title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Overview
text: Expository Definitions of Fueter regularity and the kernel, with explicit statements and proofs. Quaternions and Fueter regularity Discussion The Cauchy–Fueter kernel is the starting point for the elliptic construction. This page fixes the conventions and collects the elementary facts needed later. Prerequisites are real multivariable calculus and quaternion multiplication.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Definition F-D2 · Left and Right Fueter Regularity
text: F-D2 Definition F-D2. Left and Right Fueter Regularity A smooth function f : U → ℍ on an open set U ⊂ ℍ is left Fueter-regular if D_(ℓ)f = 0 , and right Fueter-regular if Dᵣf = 0 on U .

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Definition F-D3 · The Cauchy–Fueter Kernel
text: F-D3 Definition F-D3. The Cauchy–Fueter Kernel The Cauchy–Fueter kernel is the function G : ℍ ∖ {0} ⟶ ℍ, G(q) = (q̄)/(|q|⁴).

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Proposition F1 · Regularity of the kernel
text: F1 Proposition F1. Regularity of the kernel [1, §4, Lemma 2] The kernel G of F-D3 is both left and right Fueter-regular on ℍ ∖ {0} . For every multi-index α ∈ ℕ₀⁴ , its real partial derivative ∂^(α)G is also both left and right regular there. Put x₀ = t and e₀ = 1 , so q = ∑_(μ = 0)³e_(μ)x_(μ) . Since D_(ℓ)q̄ = 4 and ∂_(x_(μ))|q|^(− 4) = − 4x_(μ)|q|^(− 6) , the product rule gives D_(ℓ)G = 4|q|^(− 4) − 4|q|^(− 6)∑_(μ = 0)³e_(μ)q̄ x_(μ) = 4|q|^(− 4) − 4|q|^(− 6)qq̄ = 0. For Dᵣ , the sum in the second term is instead ∑_(μ)q̄ e_(μ)x_(μ) = q̄q , with the same result. Real partial derivatives commute with both constant-coefficient operators, which proves the final assertion.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Lemma F2 · Parity, homogeneity, and derivative bounds
text: F2 Lemma F2. Parity, homogeneity, and derivative bounds For every α ∈ ℕ₀⁴ , there is a constant C_(α) such that, for all q ≠ 0 and all real a > 0 , ∂^(α)G(aq), = a^(− 3 − |α|)∂^(α)G(q),; ∂^(α)G( − q), = ( − 1)^(|α| + 1)∂^(α)G(q),; |∂^(α)G(q)|, ≤ C_(α)|q|^(− 3 − |α|). In particular, G is odd, each Gⱼ is even, and Gⱼ(q) = − (eⱼ)/(|q|⁴) − (4xⱼq̄)/(|q|⁶). The defining formula gives G(aq) = a^(− 3)G(q) and G( − q) = − G(q) . Differentiating these identities in the real coordinates proves the homogeneity and parity formulas. The smooth function ∂^(α)G is bounded on the compact unit sphere. Write q = |q|u with |u| = 1 and apply homogeneity to obtain the bound. Finally, the formula for Gⱼ follows from ∂_(xⱼ)q̄ = − eⱼ and ∂_(xⱼ)|q|^(− 4) = − 4xⱼ|q|^(− 6) .

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Quaternions and coordinates
text: Quaternions and coordinates Let ℍ be the real quaternion algebra with basis (1,e₁,e₂,e₃) = (1,i,j,k) and multiplication i² = j² = k² = ijk = − 1 . Write q = t + e₁x₁ + e₂x₂ + e₃x₃, x₀ = t, e₀ = 1. For q = t + e₁x₁ + e₂x₂ + e₃x₃ , write its quaternionic conjugate and Euclidean norm as q̄ = t − e₁x₁ − e₂x₂ − e₃x₃, |q| = (t² + x₁² + x₂² + x₃²)^(1/2). The multiplication relations give qq̄ = q̄q = |q|² , since the mixed imaginary terms cancel in pairs. All partial derivatives below are ordinary real derivatives in these fixed coordinates.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: The regularity equation
text: The regularity equation For an open set U ⊂ ℍ and a smooth function f : U → ℍ , define D_(ℓ)f = ∂ₜf + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼ∂_(xⱼ)f, Dᵣf = ∂ₜf + ∑_(j = 1)³(∂_(xⱼ)f)eⱼ. Definition F-D2. Left and Right Fueter Regularity A smooth function f : U → ℍ on an open set U ⊂ ℍ is left Fueter-regular if D_(ℓ)f = 0 , and right Fueter-regular if Dᵣf = 0 on U . “Regular” in these articles refers to Fueter regularity, with the side specified when needed. Discussion Multiplying either operator by a nonzero real scalar does not change its kernel. The side on which a quaternionic coefficient acts matters. Example. Products need not preserve left regularity The constant i and z₂ = tj − x₂ are left regular, since D_(ℓ)i = 0 and D_(ℓ)z₂ = j − j = 0 . But D_(ℓ)(iz₂) = ij − ji = 2k ≠ 0. Thus pointwise multiplication does not preserve left regularity.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: The Cauchy–Fueter kernel
text: The Cauchy–Fueter kernel Definition F-D3. The Cauchy–Fueter Kernel The Cauchy–Fueter kernel is the function G : ℍ ∖ {0} ⟶ ℍ, G(q) = (q̄)/(|q|⁴). Write Gⱼ = ∂_(xⱼ)G for j = 1,2,3 . There is no surface-area factor in this normalization. Proposition F1. Regularity of the kernel [1, §4, Lemma 2] The kernel G of F-D3 is both left and right Fueter-regular on ℍ ∖ {0} . For every multi-index α ∈ ℕ₀⁴ , its real partial derivative ∂^(α)G is also both left and right regular there.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Derivatives and decay
text: Derivatives and decay Lemma F2. Parity, homogeneity, and derivative bounds For every α ∈ ℕ₀⁴ , there is a constant C_(α) such that, for all q ≠ 0 and all real a > 0 , ∂^(α)G(aq), = a^(− 3 − |α|)∂^(α)G(q),; ∂^(α)G( − q), = ( − 1)^(|α| + 1)∂^(α)G(q),; |∂^(α)G(q)|, ≤ C_(α)|q|^(− 3 − |α|). In particular, G is odd, each Gⱼ is even, and Gⱼ(q) = − (eⱼ)/(|q|⁴) − (4xⱼq̄)/(|q|⁶). Discussion A four-dimensional lattice sum with decay |λ|^(− p) converges absolutely for p > 4 , as shown in E1. The first derivatives Gⱼ are at the borderline p = 4 . The elliptic construction gains another power of decay by subtracting a constant term. Discussion. Sources and next reading Fueter's foundational papers and Sudbery's exposition are listed in the literature guide. The conventions used here are given with conjugation and norm, regularity and the kernel; the arguments above establish the displayed identities in those conventions. Continue to Quaternionic elliptic functions.

title: Quaternions and Fueter regularity
heading: Further constructions
text: Further constructions Discussion On the ball, the regular equation has weighted symmetric-spinor realizations of discrete series and a Hardy-space realization of a limit of discrete series. For differential geometry, mixed left/right pairings produce closed three-forms. These articles use the conventions fixed here.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Overview
text: Expository Precise lattice constructions, propositions, and corollaries with separately attached proofs. Quaternionic elliptic functions Discussion Summing translates of derivatives of the Cauchy–Fueter kernel produces quaternionic analogues of Weierstrass functions. This article develops three periodic functions and a zeta function with additive quasi-periods. Prerequisites are the kernel and Fueter regularity, Taylor's theorem, and uniform convergence of differentiated series.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Construction E-C1 · Regularized first-derivative lattice sums
text: E-C1 Construction E-C1. Regularized first-derivative lattice sums [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] For a full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ , j ∈ {1,2,3} , and q ∈ ℍ ∖ L , form the series ℘_(L,j)(q) = Gⱼ(q) + ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))[Gⱼ(q + λ) − Gⱼ(λ)].

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Proposition E1 · Convergence and regularity
text: E1 Proposition E1. Convergence and regularity [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . The series in E-C1 converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of ℍ ∖ L . It may be differentiated term by term to every real order, with locally uniform convergence of the differentiated series. Its sum is both left and right Fueter-regular. For every ω ∈ L , the function q ⟼ ℘_(L,j)(q) − Gⱼ(q − ω) extends to a smooth, left and right regular function on a neighborhood of ω . For a compact set K ⊂ ℍ ∖ L , choose R with |q| ≤ R on K . If |λ| > 2R , the segment from λ to λ + q stays at distance at least |λ|/2 from 0 . The derivative bound from the foundations page and the mean-value estimate give |Gⱼ(λ + q) − Gⱼ(λ)| ≤ CR|λ|^(− 5). A full-rank lattice has O(r⁴) points in a ball of radius r : write L = Aℤ⁴ for an invertible real matrix A and use equivalence of norms. Summing over dyadic shells now shows ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))|λ|^(− p) < ∞ for p > 4 . This proves absolute, locally uniform convergence. After m ≥ 1 real derivatives, the constant subtraction vanishes and each tail term is bounded by C_(K,m)|λ|^(− 4 − m) . All differentiated series therefore converge locally uniformly. The finitely many terms omitted from these tail estimates are smooth away from their singularities. The standard theorem on locally uniform convergence of derivatives permits differentiation of the sum. Every summand is left and right regular by F1, including the subtracted constant. Termwise differentiation proves regularity of the sum. In a small ball around any lattice point, remove its one singular summand; the remaining series and its derivatives converge uniformly and are regular there.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Proposition E2 · Parity and periodicity
text: E2 Proposition E2. Parity and periodicity [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . For all q ∈ ℍ ∖ L and ω ∈ L , ℘_(L,j)( − q) = ℘_(L,j)(q), ℘_(L,j)(q + ω) = ℘_(L,j)(q). Every first real partial derivative of ℘_(L,j) is the absolutely convergent sum ∂_(x_(μ))℘_(L,j)(q) = ∑_(λ ∈ L)∂_(x_(μ))Gⱼ(q + λ), μ = 0,1,2,3, x₀ = t. Reindexing this convergent sum shows that the derivatives are L -periodic. Hence H_(ω)(q) = ℘_(L,j)(q + ω) − ℘_(L,j)(q) has zero real gradient. The complement of a discrete lattice in ℝ⁴ is path connected, so H_(ω) is a constant c_(ω) . Since Gⱼ is even, reindexing the absolutely convergent defining series by λ ↦ − λ shows that ℘_(L,j) is even. Consequently H_(ω)( − q − ω) = ℘_(L,j)( − q) − ℘_(L,j)( − q − ω) = − H_(ω)(q). Both sides are constant in q , so c_(ω) = − c_(ω) , and therefore c_(ω) = 0 .

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Construction E-C2 · Subtraction of the first Taylor polynomial
text: E-C2 Construction E-C2. Subtraction of the first Taylor polynomial [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. For λ ∈ L^(∗) and q = t + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼxⱼ , let the real differential at λ act by dG_(λ)[q] = t ∂ₜG(λ) + ∑_(j = 1)³xⱼGⱼ(λ). For q ∈ ℍ ∖ L , form ζ_(L)(q) = G(q) + ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))[G(λ + q) − G(λ) − dG_(λ)[q]].

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Lemma E-L1 · Comparison with the regular linear coordinates
text: E-L1 Lemma E-L1. Comparison with the regular linear coordinates For λ ∈ ℍ ∖ {0} and q = t + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼxⱼ , put zⱼ(q) = teⱼ − xⱼ . Then dG_(λ)[q] = − ∑_(j = 1)³Gⱼ(λ)zⱼ(q). Right regularity gives ∂ₜG(λ) = − ∑ⱼGⱼ(λ)eⱼ . Substitute this into the definition of dG_(λ)[q] in E-C2 and use that t,xⱼ are real.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Proposition E3 · Convergence, derivatives, and quasi-periods
text: E3 Proposition E3. Convergence, derivatives, and quasi-periods [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. The series in E-C2 converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ ∖ L , as do all its termwise real derivatives. Its sum is odd, is both left and right Fueter-regular, and for j ∈ {1,2,3} satisfies ∂_(xⱼ)ζ_(L)(q) = ℘_(L,j)(q) (q ∉ L). There is a unique additive map η_(L) : L → ℍ such that, for every ω ∈ L and every q ∉ L , ζ_(L)(q + ω) − ζ_(L)(q) = η_(L)(ω). Taylor's theorem bounds each bracket, uniformly on a compact set, by C_(K)|λ|^(− 5) , since the second derivatives of G have degree − 5 . For first derivatives the summands are differences of first derivatives of G , again with decay |λ|^(− 5) . Derivatives of order m ≥ 2 have decay |λ|^(− 3 − m) . The argument in E1 proves convergence and permits all termwise differentiation. The first Taylor polynomial of a regular function is regular: applying either first-order constant-coefficient operator to it gives that operator applied to G , evaluated at λ , which is zero. The series is therefore left and right regular. Because G is odd and dG_(− λ) = dG_(λ) , replacing λ by − λ proves oddness of ζ_(L) . Differentiating with respect to xⱼ gives exactly the defining series for ℘_(L,j) . Now put F_(ω)(q) = ζ_(L)(q + ω) − ζ_(L)(q) . By E2, all three spatial derivatives of F_(ω) vanish. Left regularity also gives ∂ₜF_(ω) = − ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼ∂_(xⱼ)F_(ω) = 0. Connectedness of ℍ ∖ L makes F_(ω) constant. Finally, splitting the increment along ω + ν into two increments proves η_(L)(ω + ν) = η_(L)(ω) + η_(L)(ν). The constant increment determines η_(L)(ω) for each ω , so the resulting map is unique.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Corollary E4 · Half-period values of zeta
text: E4 Corollary E4. Half-period values of zeta For a full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and ω ∈ L with ω/2 ∉ L , η_(L)(ω) = 2ζ_(L)(ω/2). Set q = − ω/2 in the quasi-period identity of E3 and use the oddness of ζ_(L) .

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Corollary E5 · Stationary points at half-periods
text: E5 Corollary E5. Stationary points at half-periods Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. For j ∈ {1,2,3} and ω ∈ L with ω/2 ∉ L , the real differential of ℘_(L,j) vanishes at ω/2 : ∂_(x_(μ))℘_(L,j)(ω/2) = 0 (μ = 0,1,2,3; x₀ = t). By E1 the derivatives exist. Differentiating the two identities in E2 shows that each first derivative is odd and L -periodic. Its values at ω/2 and − ω/2 are therefore both equal and negatives of one another, so they vanish.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Corollary E6 · Real dilation
text: E6 Corollary E6. Real dilation Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice, a > 0 a real number, and j ∈ {1,2,3} . For all q ∉ L and ω ∈ L , ℘_(aL,j)(aq), = a^(− 4)℘_(L,j)(q),; ζ_(aL)(aq), = a^(− 3)ζ_(L)(q),; η_(aL)(aω), = a^(− 3)η_(L)(ω). Reindex each convergent series using aλ ∈ aL and apply F2. In the zeta subtraction, dG_(aλ)[aq] = a^(− 3)dG_(λ)[q] , since each first derivative of G has degree − 4 . Thus every bracket has the stated weight. Apply the resulting zeta identity to the difference at q + ω and q and use E3 to obtain the identity for η .

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: 1. The lattice
text: 1. The lattice Fix a full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ , written as L = ℤω₀ + ℤω₁ + ℤω₂ + ℤω₃, where the four generators are linearly independent over ℝ . Put L^(∗) = L ∖ {0} . Use the fixed coordinates q = t + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼxⱼ and the functions G(q) = (q̄)/(|q|⁴), Gⱼ = ∂_(xⱼ)G, j = 1,2,3. Each bracket in the following lattice sums is a single summand; convergence is asserted for the bracketed sums. Discussion The naive sum of translates of Gⱼ has borderline decay |λ|^(− 4) in four dimensions. Subtracting the constant Gⱼ(λ) gains an extra power of decay. The individual terms inside a bracket must not be split into divergent lattice sums.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: 2. The elliptic functions
text: 2. The elliptic functions Construction E-C1. Regularized first-derivative lattice sums [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] For a full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ , j ∈ {1,2,3} , and q ∈ ℍ ∖ L , form the series ℘_(L,j)(q) = Gⱼ(q) + ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))[Gⱼ(q + λ) − Gⱼ(λ)]. Discussion Here “elliptic” means lattice-periodic and Fueter-regular away from isolated singularities. E1 and E2 supply these properties for E-C1. Proposition E1. Convergence and regularity [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . The series in E-C1 converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of ℍ ∖ L . It may be differentiated term by term to every real order, with locally uniform convergence of the differentiated series. Its sum is both left and right Fueter-regular. For every ω ∈ L , the function q ⟼ ℘_(L,j)(q) − Gⱼ(q − ω) extends to a smooth, left and right regular function on a neighborhood of ω . Proposition E2. Parity and periodicity [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . For all q ∈ ℍ ∖ L and ω ∈ L , ℘_(L,j)( − q) = ℘_(L,j)(q), ℘_(L,j)(q + ω) = ℘_(L,j)(q). Discussion The proof reindexes the absolutely convergent derivative series, then uses evenness to remove the possible constant increment. It does not reindex an unregularized borderline sum.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: 3. The zeta function
text: 3. The zeta function Construction E-C2. Subtraction of the first Taylor polynomial [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. For λ ∈ L^(∗) and q = t + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼxⱼ , let the real differential at λ act by dG_(λ)[q] = t ∂ₜG(λ) + ∑_(j = 1)³xⱼGⱼ(λ). For q ∈ ℍ ∖ L , form ζ_(L)(q) = G(q) + ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))[G(λ + q) − G(λ) − dG_(λ)[q]]. Lemma E-L1. Comparison with the regular linear coordinates For λ ∈ ℍ ∖ {0} and q = t + ∑_(j = 1)³eⱼxⱼ , put zⱼ(q) = teⱼ − xⱼ . Then dG_(λ)[q] = − ∑_(j = 1)³Gⱼ(λ)zⱼ(q). Discussion E-L1 expresses the real Taylor subtraction using regular linear coordinates. The order of quaternionic multiplication is explicit in the formula. Proposition E3. Convergence, derivatives, and quasi-periods [1]; [2, §4, eq. (12), p. 1019] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. The series in E-C2 converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ ∖ L , as do all its termwise real derivatives. Its sum is odd, is both left and right Fueter-regular, and for j ∈ {1,2,3} satisfies ∂_(xⱼ)ζ_(L)(q) = ℘_(L,j)(q) (q ∉ L). There is a unique additive map η_(L) : L → ℍ such that, for every ω ∈ L and every q ∉ L , ζ_(L)(q + ω) − ζ_(L)(q) = η_(L)(ω). Discussion The map η_(L) is the first period datum supplied by the construction. Further relations among its values require additional statements and proofs.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: 4. Consequences and examples
text: 4. Consequences and examples Corollary E4. Half-period values of zeta For a full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and ω ∈ L with ω/2 ∉ L , η_(L)(ω) = 2ζ_(L)(ω/2). Corollary E5. Stationary points at half-periods Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice. For j ∈ {1,2,3} and ω ∈ L with ω/2 ∉ L , the real differential of ℘_(L,j) vanishes at ω/2 : ∂_(x_(μ))℘_(L,j)(ω/2) = 0 (μ = 0,1,2,3; x₀ = t). Corollary E6. Real dilation Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice, a > 0 a real number, and j ∈ {1,2,3} . For all q ∉ L and ω ∈ L , ℘_(aL,j)(aq), = a^(− 4)℘_(L,j)(q),; ζ_(aL)(aq), = a^(− 3)ζ_(L)(q),; η_(aL)(aω), = a^(− 3)η_(L)(ω). Example. The standard lattice For L₀ = ℤ + ℤi + ℤj + ℤk , E2 gives periods 1,i,j,k . Additivity in E3 determines η_(L₀) from its four values on these generators. Since 1/2 ∉ L₀ , E4 gives η_(L₀)(1) = 2ζ_(L₀)(1/2) and E5 gives d℘_(L₀,j)(1/2) = 0 for j = 1,2,3 . The zeta value is expressed by a convergent series here; no numerical evaluation is asserted. Discussion E6 describes real dilation. An action by general quaternions requires a separate transformation statement. Discussion. Open directions

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: 5. Further questions
text: 5. Further questions Which identities relate quasi-periods to the lattice and the kernel's singularity? How do extra multiplication symmetries act on these functions? How are the lattice coefficients related to harmonic theta series? These questions are developed as open directions in From lattice sums to number theory. Discussion. Sources and scope

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Sources and scope
text: Sources and scope The quaternionic Weierstrass construction is classical work of Fueter. Kraußhar's [2, §4, p. 1019, eq. (12)] displays the regularized first-derivative sum and attributes its quaternionic case to Fueter's 1939 paper. See the literature guide for the references and the remaining comparison with Fueter's original notation. This article supplies explicit arguments for its boxed formulations and makes no novelty claim. Each result carries its own review and formal-verification status.

title: Quaternionic elliptic functions
heading: Representations and special values of the coefficients
text: Representations and special values of the coefficients Discussion The higher derivative identities express the regular part of these elliptic functions through convergent lattice sums. Varying the lattice gives Eisenstein functions on SL₄, while harmonic theta series express their scalar components through critical L-values. For a concrete first example, TH5 computes the coefficient of x₁² in the regular part of ℘_(L₀,1) for L₀ = ℤ + ℤi + ℤj + ℤk as 96iL(η(2τ)¹²,5) , with a proof of the exact modular identity and its normalization. A separate group action, by Möbius transformations of the ball, leads to discrete series and the ordinary Fueter Hardy limit. The connections among these actions are a source of further questions.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Overview
text: Expository Eisenstein sums and coefficient identities, separated from open research directions. From lattice sums to number theory Discussion The elliptic construction starts from an arbitrary full-rank lattice. Its coefficients supply a first connection to lattice Eisenstein sums. The precise statements below lead to representations and special values, followed by questions about arithmetic multiplication and periods.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Construction N-C1 · Higher Eisenstein and elliptic sums
text: N-C1 Construction N-C1. Higher Eisenstein and elliptic sums [1, §§3–5] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and let ν ∈ ℕ₀³ satisfy |ν| ≥ 2 . Form E_(ν)(L) = ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))G_(ν)(λ), ℘_(L,ν)(q) = ∑_(λ ∈ L)G_(ν)(q + λ) − E_(ν)(L) (q ∉ L).

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Proposition N2 · Convergence and periodicity of the higher sums
text: N2 Proposition N2. Convergence and periodicity of the higher sums [1, §§3–5] For every full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and every ν ∈ ℕ₀³ with |ν| ≥ 2 , the Eisenstein series in N-C1 converges absolutely. The defining series for ℘_(L,ν) converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ ∖ L . For every ω ∈ L and q ∉ L , ℘_(L,ν)(q + ω) = ℘_(L,ν)(q). F2 gives decay |q|^(− 3 − |ν|) , with exponent at least 5 . The lattice-count estimate from the proof of E1 therefore proves absolute convergence, uniformly on compact sets away from the lattice for the translated sum. Absolute convergence permits reindexing λ ↦ λ + ω , which proves periodicity.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Proposition N1 · Coefficients at the singularity
text: N1 Proposition N1. Coefficients at the singularity [1, §§3–5] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . Let hⱼ be the smooth extension near 0 of ℘_(L,j) − Gⱼ supplied by E1. For every μ ∈ ℕ₀³ with |μ| ≥ 1 , ∂^(μ)hⱼ(0) = E_(μ + ϵⱼ)(L). Differentiate the convergent series for hⱼ from E1 and evaluate at q = 0 . The subtracted constants disappear, leaving ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))G_(μ + ϵⱼ)(λ) . This converges absolutely since |μ + ϵⱼ| ≥ 2 .

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Corollary N3 · Parity cancellation
text: N3 Corollary N3. Parity cancellation For every full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and every ν ∈ ℕ₀³ with even |ν| ≥ 2 , E_(ν)(L) = 0. By F2, G_(ν) is odd when |ν| is even. The terms at λ and − λ cancel, and absolute convergence from N2 justifies pairing them.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Higher derivatives and Eisenstein sums
text: Higher derivatives and Eisenstein sums For ν = (n₁,n₂,n₃) ∈ ℕ₀³ , set |ν| = n₁ + n₂ + n₃, ∂^(ν) = ∂_(x₁)^(n₁)∂_(x₂)^(n₂)∂_(x₃)^(n₃), G_(ν) = ∂^(ν)G. Write ϵⱼ for the multi-index with a single 1 in position j , for j ∈ {1,2,3} . Construction N-C1. Higher Eisenstein and elliptic sums [1, §§3–5] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and let ν ∈ ℕ₀³ satisfy |ν| ≥ 2 . Form E_(ν)(L) = ∑_(λ ∈ L^(∗))G_(ν)(λ), ℘_(L,ν)(q) = ∑_(λ ∈ L)G_(ν)(q + λ) − E_(ν)(L) (q ∉ L). Proposition N2. Convergence and periodicity of the higher sums [1, §§3–5] For every full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and every ν ∈ ℕ₀³ with |ν| ≥ 2 , the Eisenstein series in N-C1 converges absolutely. The defining series for ℘_(L,ν) converges absolutely and locally uniformly on ℍ ∖ L . For every ω ∈ L and q ∉ L , ℘_(L,ν)(q + ω) = ℘_(L,ν)(q). Proposition N1. Coefficients at the singularity [1, §§3–5] Let L ⊂ ℍ be a full-rank lattice and j ∈ {1,2,3} . Let hⱼ be the smooth extension near 0 of ℘_(L,j) − Gⱼ supplied by E1. For every μ ∈ ℕ₀³ with |μ| ≥ 1 , ∂^(μ)hⱼ(0) = E_(μ + ϵⱼ)(L). Corollary N3. Parity cancellation For every full-rank lattice L ⊂ ℍ and every ν ∈ ℕ₀³ with even |ν| ≥ 2 , E_(ν)(L) = 0. Discussion These are foundational identities, with no novelty claim. They explain how higher Eisenstein sums enter the regular part of the elliptic construction. Among the absolutely convergent sums, order 2 vanishes by N3, so order 3 is the first order not eliminated by this parity argument. For related lattice sums and Laurent coefficients, see [1], §§4–5.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Eisenstein representations
text: Eisenstein representations Discussion Varying the lattice produces Eisenstein functions on SL₄. Their irreducible module, inducing parameter, and compact types are established there with proofs. This lattice action differs from the Möbius action on regular functions in the discrete-series and Hardy constructions.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Harmonic theta series
text: Harmonic theta series Discussion The kernel derivatives have harmonic polynomial numerators. Their convergent lattice sums admit a Mellin formula; even integral lattices give harmonic theta cusp forms and critical L-values. The cubic example identifies a specific coefficient with the value at five of the weight-six newform η(2τ)¹². The order-one sum and its proposed connection to quasi-periods still need a regularization theorem. Other arithmetic lattices, Hecke decompositions, and algebraic period normalizations remain open directions. Discussion. Open directions — no theorem asserted

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Multiplication and arithmetic lattices
text: Multiplication and arithmetic lattices Lattices with an action by elements of a quaternion algebra suggest transformation laws for the elliptic functions and quasi-periods. The action and its hypotheses need precise statements. A transformation identity and an independent arithmetic constraint are different conclusions.

title: From lattice sums to number theory
heading: Period relations
text: Period relations The additivity of η_(L) is part of E3. Relating it to a residue or to integrals on ℍ/L requires further statements fixing normalization, orientation, and left/right regularity. The closed pairings and pullback identities supply local results; quotient cohomology remains open. The literature guide collects sources and further reading. These questions remain in the research notebook for investigation.

title: About this wiki
heading: Overview
text: Purpose, mathematical evidence, attribution, and how the collection grows. A growing mathematical reference This wiki is the readable output of a Math 2.0 research project: a place to collect a coherent body of useful mathematics, whether established or new, and make its reasoning available to readers. Its first subject is quaternionic analysis and its connections to number theory. A reader should be able to enter through a definition, follow a construction through its proof, and discover related questions without reconstructing a research conversation.

title: About this wiki
heading: What a page contains
text: What a page contains The mathematical core consists of separately boxed definitions, constructions, and results. A result states its hypotheses and conclusion, names the definitions and earlier results it uses, and carries its own formulation version and review status. Its proof appears directly beneath it. Discussion provides motivation, interpretation, and context. Examples and open questions are labeled separately. The “Hide discussion” control lets readers inspect the statements and proofs without that commentary. A result must remain interpretable from its stated hypotheses and explicit dependencies; essential assumptions must not be buried in discussion. A box identifies a precise mathematical claim. It does not certify that claim. Constructions link to the results establishing their well-definedness; theorem, lemma, proposition, and corollary labels do not turn an unreviewed argument into a checked proof. Pages are organized by subject and mathematical dependence. A single research investigation may contribute to several articles; an article may draw on several investigations.

title: About this wiki
heading: Evidence belongs to a statement
text: Evidence belongs to a statement A proof supplied is an explicit mathematical argument available to inspect. It may still contain a gap or error. Independently reviewed means a recorded review of the exact statement and argument; it does not mean merely that the page has been edited. Formally verified means an exact statement checked by a proof assistant, with its source, assumptions, toolchain, and checking evidence linked. None of the results in this published collection currently carries that status. Definitions, conjectures, open questions, and numerical observations should be recognizable as such. Computation can support or refute a claim within its tested scope; it does not silently become a general proof.

title: About this wiki
heading: Attribution and new contributions
text: Attribution and new contributions Existing constructions and results are attributed to their sources. A proposed new contribution needs both mathematical justification and a separate assessment of its relationship to the literature. The initial construction pages make no claim of novelty. The articles are written with AI assistance and include explicit mathematical derivations. Review status is recorded for each result; a linked review record identifies whether the reviewer was an AI agent or a human mathematician and states the scope of the check. The literature guide records sources, their relevance, and how closely they have been inspected.

title: About this wiki
heading: How the collection grows
text: How the collection grows The working research notebook preserves exploratory arguments, corrections, failed approaches, and branches that have not yet been followed. The wiki turns developed material into exposition for readers. Open directions can appear here with their status made explicit. As results change, their statements, proofs, dependencies, and evidence are revised together. Earlier formulations remain recoverable in version history.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Overview
text: Expository Weighted regular spinors, explicit group actions, compact types, and proofs of irreducibility and square-integrability. Fueter regularity and discrete series Discussion Fueter regularity realizes an entire family of discrete-series representations when the coefficients are compatible symmetric spinors. The construction below gives the Hilbert spaces, the group action, and the proofs. The case of one unrestricted quaternionic value is the Hardy limit discussed in the following article.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Proposition DS1 · The spinor-to-Fueter isometry
text: DS1 Proposition DS1. The spinor-to-Fueter isometry cf. [1, §§2–3] For n ≥ 1 , Tₙ : Vₙ → Wₙ is a complex-linear isometric isomorphism, with inverse A − jB ↦ XA + YB . In particular dim_(ℂ) Wₙ = n + 1 . The polynomials f_(X)/n and f_(Y)/n satisfy the compatibility condition, and for h = A − jB ∈ Wₙ the inverse is particularly simple: , Tₙ^(− 1)h = XA + YB., (C5) Differentiating (C5), using A_(Y) = B_(X) and Euler's identity, gives (XA + YB)_(X) = nA and (XA + YB)_(Y) = nB . This proves the inverse formula. For a monomial X^(n − k)Y^(k) , the squared norm of Tₙ 's image is ((n − k)²)/(((n − 1)/(k))) + (k²)/(((n − 1)/(k − 1))) = (n²)/(((n)/(k))), with absent endpoint terms omitted. Images of distinct monomials are orthogonal for the underlying complex inner product, proving the isometry.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Definition DS-D2 · Weighted Regular Functions
text: DS-D2 Definition DS-D2. Weighted Regular Functions For an integer n ≥ 2 , put Cₙ = n(n − 1)/π² . The weighted regular space consists of the smooth functions in , ℋₙ = {h : B ⟶ Wₙ : Dₗh = 0, ‖h‖_(ℋₙ)² = Cₙ∫_(B)∑_(k = 0)^(n − 1)(|hₖ(q)|²)/(((n − 1)/(k)))s(q)^(n − 2) dv(q) < ∞},, (C2) where Dₗ = ∂ₜ + i∂ₓ + j∂_(y) + k∂_(z) acts coefficientwise.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Construction DS-C1 · The Möbius Representation
text: DS-C1 Construction DS-C1. The Möbius Representation [1, §§2.1–3.4] Define , (Πₙ(γ)h)(q) = |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1)h(q^(′)) S_(n − 1)(ι(J^(− 1)))^(t)., (C3) The matrix entries multiply quaternion coefficients on the right, while J^(− 1) multiplies on the left. On polynomial spinors the corresponding formula is , (πₙ(γ)f)(q) = |J|^(− 2)τₙ(J^(− 1))f(q^(′))., (C7)

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Theorem DS2 · Completeness, covariance, and unitarity
text: DS2 Theorem DS2. Completeness, covariance, and unitarity [1, §§2.1–3.4] For n ≥ 2 , ℋₙ and ℬₙ are nonzero complete Hilbert spaces. Their distributional kernels have smooth harmonic representatives. The formulas in DS-C1 define strongly continuous unitary group representations, and Tₙπₙ = ΠₙTₙ . If Dₗ(Tₙf) = 0 distributionally, apply D̄ₗ = ∂ₜ − i∂ₓ − j∂_(y) − k∂_(z) . Since D̄ₗDₗ = Δ and Tₙ is a fixed injective linear map, Δ f = 0 distributionally. Weyl's lemma gives a smooth harmonic representative. In particular all its coefficient functions are harmonic. For a convergent sequence in the weighted L² norm, convergence also holds in L² on each compact subset, because the weight is strictly positive there. The distributional equation passes to the limit, as does the fixed algebraic fibre constraint. Consequently (C6) is closed and complete. Interior harmonic estimates make evaluation at each point continuous. This also justifies differentiating and averaging its vectors inside the ball. Quaternion arguments of τₙ always mean their ι matrices. The cocycle J(g₁g₂,q) = J(g₁,g₂q)J(g₂,q) proves the group law with the indicated inverse-element convention. The polynomial chain rule shows Tₙπₙ(γ) = Πₙ(γ)Tₙ, including the inverse and transpose in (C3). For covariance of the differential equation, lift f to , F_(f)(g) = |d|^(− 2)τₙ(d^(− 1))f(g ⋅ 0), g = (a, b; c, d)., (C8) Here the blocks belong to g , not its inverse. This is a right-K-equivariant function, F_(f)(gk) = τₙ(k_(R))^(− 1)F_(f)(g) . The connection and weight theorem establishes , 24(DF_(f))(σ(q)) = s^((n + 4)/2)Dₗ(Tₙf), F_(f)(σ(q)) = s^((n + 2)/2)f(q)., (C9) Left translation on the lifted space commutes with D , so it preserves the kernel and gives (C7). The connection and its curvature are included in that calculation. For unitarity, write r = |J| . Then s(q^(′)) = s(q)/r², dv(q^(′)) = r^(− 8)dv(q), ‖|J|^(− 2)τₙ(J^(− 1))v‖² = r^(− 2n − 4)‖v‖². These factors cancel exactly against the weight s^(n − 2) in the change of variables. Hence (C7), and therefore (C3), are unitary. Strong continuity follows first on compactly supported continuous functions in the ambient weighted L² space by change of variables, then by density and unitarity; the closed invariant kernel inherits it. Nonzeroness follows from the constant Vₙ -valued functions.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Theorem DS3 · Irreducibility by compact averaging
text: DS3 Theorem DS3. Irreducibility by compact averaging [1, §§2.1–3.4] For each n ≥ 2 , the representation on ℬₙ , equivalently on ℋₙ , is irreducible. The group translates of the constant Vₙ have dense span. The compact action is , (πₙ(a,b)f)(q) = τₙ(b)f(a^(− 1)qb)., (C10) Average over the first factor, with Haar probability measure: , (P_(L)f)(q) = ∫_(Sp (1))f(a^(− 1)q) da = f(0)., (C11) For q ≠ 0 , this is the spherical mean of the harmonic function f over the sphere of radius |q| ; for q = 0 it is immediate. Thus P_(L) is the orthogonal projection onto the constant Vₙ . The second compact factor acts irreducibly on those constants by τₙ . Let M be a nonzero closed G -invariant subspace. Choose f ∈ M and a point p with f(p) ≠ 0 . Transitivity and the invertible fibre multiplier give a translate πₙ(g)f nonzero at 0 . Averaging that vector by P_(L) gives a nonzero constant in M . Its second-compact-factor orbit spans the entire constant Vₙ , so M contains every constant. If M were proper, unitarity would make M^(⟂) another nonzero closed invariant subspace. The same argument would put all constants in M^(⟂) , a contradiction. Therefore the representation is irreducible. Equivalently, the translates of its constant Vₙ span a dense subspace.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Theorem DS4 · A closed embedding into the regular representation
text: DS4 Theorem DS4. A closed embedding into the regular representation [1, §§2–3] For n ≥ 2 , the representation belongs to the discrete series of Sp (1,1) . For any nonzero v ∈ Vₙ , let cᵥ be its constant function and put (Wᵥf)(g) = ⟨ πₙ(g^(− 1))f,cᵥ ⟩ , with inner product linear in the first argument. This map has closed image in L²(G) and satisfies ‖Wᵥf‖_(L²(G))² = (‖v‖²)/((n + 1)Cₙ)‖f‖_(ℬₙ)² for the Haar measure specified in the proof. Fix Haar measure by ∫_(G)Φ (g) dg = ∫_(B)∫_(K)Φ (σ(q)k) dk s(q)^(− 4)dv(q), ∫_(K)dk = 1 in this disintegration convention. The base measure is invariant. Let v ∈ Vₙ be nonzero and cᵥ its constant function. Use a complex inner product linear in the first argument. Harmonic mean values and the probability measure give ⟨ f,cᵥ ⟩_(ℬₙ) = ⟨ f(0),v ⟩_(Vₙ). The matrix-coefficient map , (Wᵥf)(g) = ⟨ πₙ(g^(− 1))f,cᵥ ⟩ = ⟨ F_(f)(g),v ⟩ , (C12) intertwines πₙ with left translation on functions on G . Schur orthogonality for the finite-dimensional irreducible τₙ gives ∫_(K)| ⟨ τₙ(k_(R))^(− 1)u,v ⟩ |²dk = (‖u‖²‖v‖²)/(n + 1). Since F_(f)(σ(q)) = s^((n + 2)/2)f(q) , we obtain the exact norm identity , ‖Wᵥf‖_(L²(G))² = (‖v‖²)/((n + 1)Cₙ) ‖f‖_(ℬₙ)²., (C13) Thus a fixed scalar multiple of Wᵥ is an isometric embedding with closed invariant image in L²(G) . Together with irreducibility, this proves that ℬₙ and ℋₙ are discrete series. For normalized v , the inverse constant in (C13) is n(n² − 1)/π² for the specified Haar measure. Its vanishing at the endpoint is consistent with the divergence proved in H4; it is not used as a substitute for that argument.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Theorem DS5 · The complete compact decomposition
text: DS5 Theorem DS5. The complete compact decomposition [1, Thm. 3.9] For n ≥ 2 , ℋₙ|_(K) ≃ ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + n). Every type occurs once. Coordinate degree m has dimension (m + 1)(m + n + 1) , and the constants form the unique minimal type V₀ ⊠ Vₙ . The same polynomial-kernel calculation holds for n = 1 and supplies the compact types of the Hardy space. Let P_(m,n) be the degree- m homogeneous polynomials in the real coordinates of q , valued in Vₙ , satisfying Dₗ(Tₙf) = 0 . Harmonicity puts this space inside SHₘ(ℝ⁴) ⊗ Vₙ ≃ Vₘ ⊠ (Vₘ ⊗ Vₙ). Here the scalar spherical harmonics on S³ ≃ Sp (1) carry the standard left/right type Vₘ ⊠ Vₘ . For the right factor set Rⱼf = ∂_(qeⱼ)f , where e₀ = 1,e₁ = i,e₂ = j,e₃ = k . On degree- m functions R₀ = mI . The infinitesimal action is dτₙ(eⱼ) + Rⱼ for j = 1,2,3 , so its Casimir is C_(R) = − n(n + 2) − m(m + 2) + 2∑_(j = 1)³dτₙ(eⱼ)Rⱼ. The equation forces the cross term to be − mn . To check this without an implicit coordinate change, put Tf = (f_(X),f_(Y))^(t) and write the flat equation as ∑_(i = 0)³ι(eᵢ)T(∂ᵢf) = 0. Multiply on the left by ι(q̄) and contract a column (A,B)^(t) to XA + YB . The result is , 0 = ∑ᵢdτₙ(q̄eᵢ)∂ᵢf = ∑_(j = 0)³dτₙ(eⱼ)Rⱼf., (C14) The last equality follows from q̄eᵢ = ∑ⱼ ⟨ qeⱼ,eᵢ ⟩ eⱼ . The j = 0 term is nmf , proving the assertion. Consequently C_(R) acts as − (m + n)(m + n + 2). The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of Vₘ ⊗ Vₙ has distinct Casimir values and contains V_(m + n) once. Hence P_(m,n) lies in Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + n) . It is nonzero: the explicit seed , fₘ(q;X,Y) = (t + ix)^(m)Xⁿ, (C15) is regular, because (∂ₜ + i∂ₓ)(t + ix)^(m) = 0 . Since the candidate compact summand is irreducible and the kernel is K -invariant, its nonzero subspace is the whole summand. Thus P_(m,n) = Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + n), dim_(ℂ) P_(m,n) = (m + 1)(m + n + 1). Harmonic functions on the ball have homogeneous harmonic expansions. Their degrees are orthogonal on every sphere, and therefore for the radial measure dμₙ . The flat first-order equation holds separately on each homogeneous term. Parseval's identity on spheres and integration in the radius show that partial sums converge in the Hilbert norm. This proves the complete direct-sum decomposition in the theorem.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Proposition DS6 · Polynomial seeds and translated constants
text: DS6 Proposition DS6. Polynomial seeds and translated constants For n ≥ 2 and m ≥ 0 , the vectors hₘ = (t + ix)^(m)X^(n − 1) span each compact type under K , have squared norm m ! /(n + 1)ₘ , and the translates of constant spinors displayed in the proof have dense span. Under Tₙ , the seed becomes the particularly simple quaternion-valued polynomial hₘ(q;X,Y) = (t + ix)^(m)X^(n − 1). Its squared norm is , ‖hₘ‖² = (m !)/((n + 1)ₘ), (n + 1)ₘ = (n + 1)(n + 2)⋯(n + m),, (C16) by the beta integral. Its K -orbit spans the entire type of degree m . Constants ( m = 0 ) are the minimal type; the two highest-weight labels increase with m , also making this the unique minimum for the usual compact highest-weight norm. An additional supply of nonpolynomial examples comes directly from translated constants. For any p ∈ B and v ∈ Vₙ , , f_(p,v)(q) = s(p)^((n + 2)/2)|1 − p̄q|^(− 2)τₙ((1 − p̄q)^(− 1))v = πₙ(σ(p))cᵥ(q)., (C17) These are regular spinors of norm ‖v‖ , and Tₙf_(p,v) are corresponding Fueter-regular vectors. Their span is dense by DS3. For the norm, put u = t² + x² and v = y² + z² . Euclidean measure becomes π²du dv after angular integration, so Cₙπ²∫_(u + v < 1)u^(m)(1 − u − v)^(n − 2)du dv = (m ! n !)/((m + n) !). For a translate, σ(p)^(− 1) has c = − p̄/√(s(p)) and d = 1/√(s(p)) ; substituting these blocks in C7 gives the displayed formula, and unitarity gives its norm.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Corollary DS7 · The first member as a pair of regular functions
text: DS7 Corollary DS7. The first member as a pair of regular functions The n = 2 representation is the space of pairs (h₀,h₁) = (a − jb,b − jc) , with a,b,c complex functions on B , satisfying coefficientwise Fueter regularity and ‖h‖² = (2)/(π²)∫_(B)(|h₀|² + |h₁|²) dv < ∞. Its minimal compact type has complex dimension three. For n = 2 , write f = a(q)X² + 2b(q)XY + c(q)Y², h = T₂f = (a − jb)X + (b − jc)Y, where a,b,c are complex-valued. Thus the representation consists exactly of pairs (h₀,h₁) = (a − jb, b − jc) that are componentwise Fueter-regular and satisfy ‖h‖² = (2)/(π²)∫_(B)(|h₀|² + |h₁|²) dv < ∞. The measure is ordinary ball volume, up to normalization. The action is fully explicit: (Π₂(γ)h)(q) = |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1)(h₀(q^(′)),h₁(q^(′)))ι(J^(− 1))^(t). Constant pairs of this form constitute the three-dimensional complex minimal K -type. The pair (t + ix,0) is a nonconstant vector, of squared norm 1/3 , in the next compact type of complex dimension 8 . All formulas follow by inserting n = 2 into the preceding definitions and theorems.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: The group and its coefficient spaces
text: The group and its coefficient spaces Put G = Sp (1,1) , K = Sp (1)_(L) × Sp (1)_(R) , B = {q ∈ ℍ : |q| < 1} , and s(q) = 1 − |q|² . Explicitly G = {g ∈ GL₂(ℍ) : g^(∗)diag (1, − 1)g = diag (1, − 1)} , where g^(∗) is conjugate transpose. Its action is gq = (aq + b)(cq + d)^(− 1) and K consists of diag (a,b) with |a| = |b| = 1 . All representations and Hilbert spaces below are complex. For quaternion coefficients, the complex scalar acts on the right. Let Vₙ = ℂ[X,Y]ₙ with (τₙ(M)p)(X,Y) = p(aX + cY,bX + dY), M = (a, b; c, d), and the norm ‖ ∑_(k = 0)ⁿcₖX^(n − k)Y^(k) ‖ₙ² = ∑_(k = 0)ⁿ(|cₖ|²)/(((n)/(k))). A quaternion acts through ι(t + ix + jy + kz) = (t + ix, y + iz; − y + iz, t − ix). Write a quaternion-valued homogeneous polynomial of auxiliary degree n − 1 as h(q;X,Y) = ∑_(k = 0)^(n − 1)hₖ(q)X^(n − 1 − k)Y^(k) = A(q;X,Y) − jB(q;X,Y), where A,B have complex coefficients. Auxiliary variables commute with quaternion coefficients. For n ≥ 1 , put , Wₙ = {A − jB : A_(Y) = B_(X)} ⊂ ℍ[X,Y]_(n − 1)., (C1) Here A,B ∈ ℂ[X,Y]_(n − 1) ; we refer to A_(Y) = B_(X) as the compatibility condition. The first compact factor acts trivially on Vₙ . Let Tₙp = p_(X) − jp_(Y) and Tₙ = Tₙ/n for n ≥ 1 . For a quaternion coefficient row of length n , use the squared norm ∑_(k = 0)^(n − 1)|hₖ|²/((n − 1)/(k)) ; the auxiliary variables X,Y commute with coefficients. Write Dₗ = ∂ₜ + i∂ₓ + j∂_(y) + k∂_(z) , coefficientwise, with x = x₁,y = x₂,z = x₃ in the foundations article. The compatibility condition is imposed pointwise for functions of q . Proposition DS1 identifies Wₙ with Vₙ and proves that its complex dimension is n + 1 . Proposition DS1. The spinor-to-Fueter isometry cf. [1, §§2–3] For n ≥ 1 , Tₙ : Vₙ → Wₙ is a complex-linear isometric isomorphism, with inverse A − jB ↦ XA + YB . In particular dim_(ℂ) Wₙ = n + 1 .

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Weighted Hilbert spaces and the action
text: Weighted Hilbert spaces and the action Use Euclidean volume dv = dt dx dy dz on B . Definition DS-D2. Weighted Regular Functions For an integer n ≥ 2 , put Cₙ = n(n − 1)/π² . The weighted regular space consists of the smooth functions in , ℋₙ = {h : B ⟶ Wₙ : Dₗh = 0, ‖h‖_(ℋₙ)² = Cₙ∫_(B)∑_(k = 0)^(n − 1)(|hₖ(q)|²)/(((n − 1)/(k)))s(q)^(n − 2) dv(q) < ∞},, (C2) where Dₗ = ∂ₜ + i∂ₓ + j∂_(y) + k∂_(z) acts coefficientwise. The polynomial-spinor model is , ℬₙ = {f ∈ L²(B,Vₙ,dμₙ) : Dₗ(Tₙf) = 0}, dμₙ = Cₙs^(n − 2)dv., (C6) Here the equation is imposed distributionally. The map Tₙ identifies ℬₙ isometrically with ℋₙ by DS1; smoothness of the distributional kernels is proved in DS2. The measure μₙ has total mass one, since polar coordinates give ∫_(B)s^(n − 2)dv = 2π²∫₀¹r³(1 − r²)^(n − 2) dr = (π²)/(n(n − 1)). For γ ∈ G , write γ^(− 1) = (a, b; c, d), q^(′) = (aq + b)(cq + d)^(− 1), J = cq + d. Let Sₘ(M) be the coefficient-column matrix of τₘ(M) in descending monomials; in particular S₁(M) = M . Regard h = (h₀,…,h_(n − 1)) as a row. Construction DS-C1. The Möbius Representation [1, §§2.1–3.4] Define , (Πₙ(γ)h)(q) = |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1)h(q^(′)) S_(n − 1)(ι(J^(− 1)))^(t)., (C3) The matrix entries multiply quaternion coefficients on the right, while J^(− 1) multiplies on the left. On polynomial spinors the corresponding formula is , (πₙ(γ)f)(q) = |J|^(− 2)τₙ(J^(− 1))f(q^(′))., (C7) Theorem DS2. Completeness, covariance, and unitarity [1, §§2.1–3.4] For n ≥ 2 , ℋₙ and ℬₙ are nonzero complete Hilbert spaces. Their distributional kernels have smooth harmonic representatives. The formulas in DS-C1 define strongly continuous unitary group representations, and Tₙπₙ = ΠₙTₙ .

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Irreducibility and discrete series
text: Irreducibility and discrete series Theorem DS3. Irreducibility by compact averaging [1, §§2.1–3.4] For each n ≥ 2 , the representation on ℬₙ , equivalently on ℋₙ , is irreducible. The group translates of the constant Vₙ have dense span. Theorem DS4. A closed embedding into the regular representation [1, §§2–3] For n ≥ 2 , the representation belongs to the discrete series of Sp (1,1) . For any nonzero v ∈ Vₙ , let cᵥ be its constant function and put (Wᵥf)(g) = ⟨ πₙ(g^(− 1))f,cᵥ ⟩ , with inner product linear in the first argument. This map has closed image in L²(G) and satisfies ‖Wᵥf‖_(L²(G))² = (‖v‖²)/((n + 1)Cₙ)‖f‖_(ℬₙ)² for the Haar measure specified in the proof.

title: Fueter regularity and discrete series
heading: Compact types and explicit vectors
text: Compact types and explicit vectors Theorem DS5. The complete compact decomposition [1, Thm. 3.9] For n ≥ 2 , ℋₙ|_(K) ≃ ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + n). Every type occurs once. Coordinate degree m has dimension (m + 1)(m + n + 1) , and the constants form the unique minimal type V₀ ⊠ Vₙ . The same polynomial-kernel calculation holds for n = 1 and supplies the compact types of the Hardy space. Proposition DS6. Polynomial seeds and translated constants For n ≥ 2 and m ≥ 0 , the vectors hₘ = (t + ix)^(m)X^(n − 1) span each compact type under K , have squared norm m ! /(n + 1)ₘ , and the translates of constant spinors displayed in the proof have dense span. Corollary DS7. The first member as a pair of regular functions The n = 2 representation is the space of pairs (h₀,h₁) = (a − jb,b − jc) , with a,b,c complex functions on B , satisfying coefficientwise Fueter regularity and ‖h‖² = (2)/(π²)∫_(B)(|h₀|² + |h₁|²) dv < ∞. Its minimal compact type has complex dimension three. Discussion This is the l = n , quaternionic-dimension-one family in [1], §§2–3. The compact-type calculation follows their Theorem 3.9; DS3–DS4 give direct arguments for irreducibility and square-integrability. The ordinary quaternion-valued endpoint is developed in The Fueter Hardy space, and the section calculation is in Connections and the Fueter equation. The local closed pairings lead to separate quotient questions.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Overview
text: Expository The nonflat bundle connection, its projected contribution, and the exact scalar weight relating the invariant and flat equations. Connections and the Fueter equation Discussion The section over the ball has a nonzero connection. After projecting to the first-order spinor operator, that contribution cancels the derivative of one specific scalar weight. This article supplies the calculation used by the representation constructions.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Proposition SC1 · Connection, curvature, and the changing frame
text: SC1 Proposition SC1. Connection, curvature, and the changing frame cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For U = F ∘ σ , the relevant compact connection is A = (dq̄ q − q̄ dq)/(2s), dA + A ∧ A = − s^(− 2)dq̄ ∧ dq. For Cᵥ = (1)/(2)(v̄q − q̄v) one has (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s∂ᵥU + dτₙ(Cᵥ)U. Direct multiplication, including the derivative of s^(− 1/2) , gives , σ^(− 1)dσ = ((dq q̄ − q dq̄)/(2s), (dq)/(s); (dq̄)/(s), (dq̄ q − q̄ dq)/(2s))., (L4) The diagonal part is the compact connection of the reductive homogeneous bundle. Its second component, the one acting on Vₙ , is , A = (dq̄ q − q̄ dq)/(2s)., (L5) The Maurer–Cartan equation gives its curvature: , dA + A ∧ A = − (dq̄ ∧ dq)/(s²) ≠ 0., (L6) For example at q = 0 , evaluation on (∂ₜ,∂ₓ) is − 2i . On Vₙ , n ≥ 1 , its action on Xⁿ is − 2inXⁿ , also nonzero. Although A vanishes at the origin in this frame, it does not vanish throughout a neighborhood and its curvature does not vanish even at the origin. Consequently a global section, or the fact that the ball is contractible, does not justify replacing covariant derivatives by ordinary derivatives in this frame. A scalar change of frame adds an exact scalar one-form to the connection and does not remove this curvature. The cancellation below occurs only after projection to the particular first-order operator. For a smooth right-K-equivariant F , use right differentiation (ξᵥF)(g) = (d)/(dε)F(g exp (εξᵥ))|₀. Factor the path through the section: σ(q)exp (εξᵥ) = σ(q_(ε))k_(ε). Its projection to the ball has derivative q₀^(′) = v − qq̄v = sv. Evaluating (L4) on that tangent vector, and comparing with the off-diagonal Lie algebra element ξᵥ , shows that the second compact component satisfies (k₀^(′))₂ = − Cᵥ, Cᵥ = (1)/(2)(v̄q − q̄v) = sA(v). Right equivariance therefore contributes the plus sign in , (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s ∂ᵥU(q) + dτₙ(Cᵥ)U(q)., (L7) Indeed F(σ(q_(ε))k_(ε)) = τₙ((k_(ε))₂^(− 1))U(q_(ε)) , whose fibre derivative is − dτₙ((k₀^(′))₂)U . For explicit comparison in real coordinates: C₁, = ix + jy + kz,, Cᵢ, = − it + jz − ky,; Cⱼ, = − iz − jt + kx,, Cₖ, = iy − jx − kt. The infinitesimal polynomial actions in (L1) are , dτₙ(i), = i(X∂_(X) − Y∂_(Y)),; dτₙ(j), = − Y∂_(X) + X∂_(Y),; dτₙ(k), = i(Y∂_(X) + X∂_(Y))., (L8) These formulas make the changing-frame contribution completely explicit.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Lemma SC2 · The projected connection term
text: SC2 Lemma SC2. The projected connection term cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For every homogeneous p ∈ Vₙ , n ≥ 1 , ∑ᵥvTₙ(dτₙ(v̄q)p) = 2(n + 1)qTₙp, ∑ᵥvTₙ(dτₙ(Cᵥ)p) = (n + 2)qTₙp. The cancellation identity in Liu–Zhang Lemma 3.5 becomes , ∑_(v ∈ {1,i,j,k})v Tₙ(dτₙ(v̄q)p) = 2(n + 1)qTₙp, p ∈ Vₙ., (L9) Here dτₙ has been extended to all quaternion matrices; in particular dτₙ(r) = nrI for real scalars r . A direct proof avoids any assumption about a flat section. For a complex 2 × 2 matrix M , put R_(M)p = (M₁₁X + M₂₁Y)p_(X) + (M₁₂X + M₂₂Y)p_(Y), Tp = ((p_(X))/(p_(Y))), E = X∂_(X) + Y∂_(Y). Expansion of the four matrices ι(v) gives the differential-operator identity , ∑ᵥι(v)T(R_(ι(v̄q))p) = 2ι(q)(E + 2)Tp., (L10) For example, with q = ζ + wj , the first component is 2ζ(Xp_(XX) + Yp_(XY) + 2p_(X)) + 2w(Xp_(XY) + Yp_(YY) + 2p_(Y)); the second component has coefficients − w̄,ζ̄ in place of ζ,w . Since Tp is homogeneous of degree n − 1 , ETp = (n − 1)Tp . This proves (L9) for every n , not just tested degrees. Now Cᵥ = v̄q − ⟨ v,q ⟩ , so (L9) and ∑ᵥv ⟨ v,q ⟩ = q give , ∑ᵥvTₙ(dτₙ(Cᵥ)p) = (n + 2)qTₙp., (L11) Thus the connection term is not zero before weighting, even after projection.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Theorem SC3 · The section weight identifies the two kernels
text: SC3 Theorem SC3. The section weight identifies the two kernels cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For n ≥ 1 , put U = s^((n + 2)/2)f . Then 24(DF)(σ(q)) = sDₗ(TₙU) + (n + 2)qTₙU = s^((n + 4)/2)Dₗ(Tₙf). Thus the lift (L2) identifies the equivariant group kernel with the ordinary Fueter equation for Tₙf and proves covariance of the ball action. Combining (L7) and (L11) proves , 24(DF)(σ(q)) = sDₗ(TₙU) + (n + 2)qTₙU., (L13) Set β = (n + 2)/2 and U = s^(β)f . Since Dₗs = − 2q , the product rule gives , 24(DF)(σ(q)) = s^(β + 1)Dₗ(Tₙf) = s^((n + 4)/2)Dₗ(Tₙf)., (L14) The term − 2βqTₙf from differentiating the scalar weight cancels (n + 2)qTₙf exactly. For n ≥ 1 , the lift (L2) identifies smooth ball functions with the specified smooth right-K-equivariant functions, and , DF = 0 on G ⟺ Dₗ(Tₙ(s^(− (n + 2)/2)F ∘ σ)) = 0 on B., (L15) The nonzero factor s^((n + 4)/2) in (L14) gives equivalence on the section. K-equivariance of the projected group operator extends vanishing from the section to all of G = σ(B)K . This is a smooth differential assertion; it makes no discrete-series claim at n = 1 . Conversely, every smooth right-equivariant F is recovered from its value on the section, since G = σ(B)K , so the lift is bijective on the specified smooth spaces. Its left translation becomes the ball action in DS-C1. Because the projected operator is left invariant, its kernel and hence the flat Fueter kernel are preserved by that action.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Corollary SC4 · The discrepancy for any other scalar weight
text: SC4 Corollary SC4. The discrepancy for any other scalar weight cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For f_(α) = s^(α)U with any real α , 24(DF)(σ(q)) = s^(− α)[sDₗ(Tₙf_(α)) + (n + 2 + 2α)qTₙf_(α)]. The zeroth-order term disappears exactly at α = − (n + 2)/2 . Insert U = s^(− α)f_(α) in SC3 and use Dₗs = − 2q . The scalar weight does not flatten the connection: its derivative cancels this particular projected term.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Proposition SC5 · Direct differentiation of the full lift
text: SC5 Proposition SC5. Direct differentiation of the full lift cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] The lift also gives the independent formula (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s^((n + 2)/2)[s∂ᵥf + dτₙ(v̄q)f − 2(n + 1) ⟨ v,q ⟩ f]. Put β = (n + 2)/2 . To see each contribution, write H_(ε) = 1 + εq̄v + O(ε²), b_(ε)d_(ε)^(− 1) = q + εsv + O(ε²). Then the lift along the right path is F(σ(q)e^(εξᵥ)) = s^(β)|H_(ε)|^(− 2)τₙ(H_(ε)^(− 1))f(q + εsv + O(ε²)). Differentiating yields , (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s^(β)[s∂ᵥf − dτₙ(q̄v)f − 2 ⟨ v,q ⟩ f] = s^(β)[s∂ᵥf + dτₙ(v̄q)f − 2(n + 1) ⟨ v,q ⟩ f]., (L17) The equality uses q̄v + v̄q = 2 ⟨ v,q ⟩ and the scalar degree n action. This agrees with the final derivative display in [1], printed p. 2991. Applying the projection and (L9) cancels the last two terms, proving (L14) up to the chosen operator normalization. It also agrees with (L7) after substituting U = s^(β)f .

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: The equivariant lift
text: The equivariant lift Let G = Sp (1,1) . B = {q ∈ ℍ : |q| < 1}, s = 1 − |q|², q = t + ix + jy + kz, K = Sp (1) × Sp (1). Write e₀ = 1,e₁ = i,e₂ = j,e₃ = k , and distinguish the group Lie algebra element ξᵥ = (0, v; v̄, 0) from the quaternion v . Use σ(q) = s^(− 1/2)(1, q; q̄, 1), Vₙ = ℂ[X,Y]ₙ, n ≥ 1. The polynomial representation and quaternion identification are , τₙ(a, b; c, d)p(X,Y) = p(aX + cY,bX + dY), Tₙp = p_(X) − jp_(Y)., (L1) Here a quaternion acts through ι(t + ix + jy + kz) = (t + ix, y + iz; − y + iz, t − ix). Thus the complex column (A,B)^(t) represents A − jB , and left quaternion multiplication has matrix ι(q) . The first compact factor acts trivially on Vₙ . The lift from a smooth ball spinor to a right-equivariant group function is , F(g) = |d|^(− 2)τₙ(d^(− 1))f(g ⋅ 0), g = (a, b; c, d)., (L2) For k = diag (k_(L),k_(R)) , the lower-right block of gk is dk_(R) , while (gk)0 = g0 . Substitution into (L2) gives F(gk) = τₙ(k_(R))^(− 1)F(g) for k ∈ K . At g = σ(q) , the lower-right entry is the positive real quaternion s^(− 1/2) . Since τₙ(r) = rⁿI for real r > 0 , (L2) gives , U(q) : = F(σ(q)) = s^((n + 2)/2)f(q), f(q) = s^(− (n + 2)/2)U(q)., (L3) For a smooth equivariant function F , write (ξᵥF)(g) = (d)/(dε)F(g exp (εξᵥ))|₀ . For n ≥ 1 and a smooth right-equivariant F : G → Vₙ , use the following normalization of the projected first-order operator: 24DF = ∑_(v ∈ {1,i,j,k})vTₙ(ξᵥF). The factor 24 is an operator normalization and does not change its kernel. The projection v ⊗ p ↦ vTₙp is K -equivariant: the polynomial chain rule intertwines the tangent action v ↦ avb^(− 1) and p ↦ τₙ(b)p with the corresponding target action. Consequently D is well-defined on the homogeneous bundle and commutes with left translations.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: The nonflat connection
text: The nonflat connection Proposition SC1. Connection, curvature, and the changing frame cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For U = F ∘ σ , the relevant compact connection is A = (dq̄ q − q̄ dq)/(2s), dA + A ∧ A = − s^(− 2)dq̄ ∧ dq. For Cᵥ = (1)/(2)(v̄q − q̄v) one has (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s∂ᵥU + dτₙ(Cᵥ)U.

title: Connections and the Fueter equation
heading: Projection and cancellation
text: Projection and cancellation Lemma SC2. The projected connection term cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For every homogeneous p ∈ Vₙ , n ≥ 1 , ∑ᵥvTₙ(dτₙ(v̄q)p) = 2(n + 1)qTₙp, ∑ᵥvTₙ(dτₙ(Cᵥ)p) = (n + 2)qTₙp. Theorem SC3. The section weight identifies the two kernels cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For n ≥ 1 , put U = s^((n + 2)/2)f . Then 24(DF)(σ(q)) = sDₗ(TₙU) + (n + 2)qTₙU = s^((n + 4)/2)Dₗ(Tₙf). Thus the lift (L2) identifies the equivariant group kernel with the ordinary Fueter equation for Tₙf and proves covariance of the ball action. Corollary SC4. The discrepancy for any other scalar weight cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] For f_(α) = s^(α)U with any real α , 24(DF)(σ(q)) = s^(− α)[sDₗ(Tₙf_(α)) + (n + 2 + 2α)qTₙf_(α)]. The zeroth-order term disappears exactly at α = − (n + 2)/2 . Proposition SC5. Direct differentiation of the full lift cf. [1, §§2.1–3.4] The lift also gives the independent formula (ξᵥF)(σ(q)) = s^((n + 2)/2)[s∂ᵥf + dτₙ(v̄q)f − 2(n + 1) ⟨ v,q ⟩ f]. Discussion The source of the lift and cancellation is [1], equation (2.8), Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.6. The proof here differentiates the moving frame explicitly. The resulting covariance is used in the discrete-series construction and in the Hardy endpoint.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Overview
text: Expository Ordinary quaternion-valued regular functions, boundary induction, and the two limits of discrete series. The Fueter Hardy space Discussion The single-quaternion case has a boundary Hilbert norm. It realizes a genuine limit of discrete series, with an explicit splitting of the spinor principal series and a precise explanation of the failure of the ball volume norm.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Definition H-D1 · The Regular Hardy Space
text: H-D1 Definition H-D1. The Regular Hardy Space The Fueter Hardy space consists of the smooth functions in ℋ₊ = {h : B → ℍ : Dₗh = 0, ‖h‖² = sup_(0 < r < 1) ∫_(S³)|h(rω)|²dσ(ω) < ∞}.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Theorem H1 · An irreducible unitary representation on ordinary regular functions
text: H1 Theorem H1. An irreducible unitary representation on ordinary regular functions [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] The Hardy boundary trace identifies ℋ₊ isometrically with a closed invariant subspace of L²(S³,ℍ) . Its action is strongly continuous, unitary and irreducible, with ℋ₊|_(K) = ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + 1). The central element − I acts by − 1 , so the representation does not descend to SO₀(4,1) . Factorization D̄ₗDₗ = Δ makes every component harmonic. Write the homogeneous expansion as h = ∑_(m ≥ 0)hₘ . Orthogonality on spheres gives ∫_(S³)|h(rω)|²dσ = ∑_(m ≥ 0)r^(2m)‖hₘ‖_(L²(S³))². The finite supremum is exactly the sum of the squared boundary norms. Thus the radial limits exist in L² , and the image is the closure of the regular polynomials. Conversely an L² sum of these homogeneous boundary terms has a harmonic Poisson extension on B ; interior convergence of derivatives preserves regularity. This identifies the complete Hardy space and its compact types by DS5 at n = 1 . The Möbius derivative on the boundary has length factor |J|^(− 2) , hence area Jacobian |J|^(− 6) . The squared norm of the fibre multiplier |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1) is also |J|^(− 6) . Change of variables makes the action unitary on all boundary L² . The cocycle proves its group law; continuity on smooth boundary functions and density prove strong continuity. SC3 preserves the regular equation. Transforms of regular polynomials are regular and smooth up to the closed ball, since cq + d never vanishes there for a fixed ball automorphism. Their boundary values therefore stay in the Hardy subspace, which is consequently invariant by closure. For irreducibility, average over the first compact factor: ∫_(Sp(1))h(a^(− 1)q)da = h(0). This is the harmonic mean-value formula. Any nonzero invariant closed subspace has a vector nonzero somewhere. Translate that point to zero, average, and obtain a nonzero constant. The second compact factor acts irreducibly on the constants, so the subspace contains all constants. Its orthogonal complement, if nonzero, would contain them too, which is impossible. Finally insert J = − 1 and q^(′) = q to compute the central action.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Proposition H-D2 · The Boundary Model of Normalized Induction
text: H-D2 Proposition H-D2. The Boundary Model of Normalized Induction [1, §3, pp. 249–250] The formula (H1) extends to a unitary representation on ℬ = L²(S³,ℍ) and realizes , I(σ,0) = Ind_(MAN)^(G) (σ ⊗ 1 ⊗ 1), (H3) with the normalized induction convention above. The boundary Jacobian of q ↦ γ^(− 1)q is |J|^(− 6) . The multiplier |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1) has squared norm |J|^(− 6) , so change of variables preserves the boundary L² norm. The group law follows from the automorphy-factor identity used in H1. At 1 , the diagonal subgroup M acts on the fibre by its standard complex two-dimensional representation. With the parameter aₜ , the positive restricted root has value t and multiplicity three, so ρ = 3/2 . For Π (aₜ) , formula (H1) uses aₜ^(− 1) and has J = e^(− t/2) at the fixed point 1 . Its multiplier is therefore e^(3t/2) , the inverse of the section character e^(− 3t/2) . These fibre actions identify the boundary model with the displayed induced representation.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Theorem H2 · The two Hardy summands of the spinor principal series
text: H2 Theorem H2. The two Hardy summands of the spinor principal series [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] For σ = V₁ of M ≃ Sp(1) , normalized induction at parameter zero splits as I(σ,0) = ℋ₊⊕︎ [ˆ]ℋ_(−), ℋ_(−) = Cℋ₊, (Cf)(ω) = ω̄f(ω̄). Both summands are irreducible and inequivalent. The second has compact types ⨁_(m ≥ 0)V_(m + 1) ⊠ Vₘ . Peter–Weyl on S³ ≃ Sp (1) and Clebsch–Gordan give , ℬ|_(K) = ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)[(Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + 1)) ⊕︎ (V_(m + 1) ⊠ Vₘ)]., (H4) The two summands can be separated explicitly by the unitary Kelvin involution (Cf)(ω) = ω̄f(ω̄), C² = 1. For k = (a,b) , CΠ (a,b)C = Π (b,a) . More generally , CΠ (g)C = Π (WgW), W = (0, 1; 1, 0)., (H5) Although W reverses the defining Hermitian form, conjugation by it preserves G . For a direct check write g^(− 1) = (a, b; c, d) and |q| = 1 . Applying CΠ (g)C gives multiplier |cq̄ + d|^(− 2)q̄(aq̄ + b)^(− 1) = |bq + a|^(− 2)(bq + a)^(− 1) and argument (cq̄ + d)(aq̄ + b)^(− 1) = (dq + c)(bq + a)^(− 1) . Here |cq̄ + d| = |aq̄ + b| = |bq + a| on the sphere. These are precisely the multiplier and argument for Π (WgW) . In particular Cℋ₊ is invariant and irreducible, with the compact factors exchanged. H1 and the preceding compact decomposition imply the orthogonal decomposition , I(σ,0) = ℋ₊⊕︎ [ˆ]ℋ_(−), ℋ_(−) = Cℋ₊, ℋ_(−)|_(K) = ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)V_(m + 1) ⊠ Vₘ., (H6) The map C is complex-linear, preserves the boundary norm, and satisfies C² = 1 . The conjugation identity proves invariance and irreducibility of the second space. Their disjoint compact types imply orthogonality, and the full compact decomposition exhausts boundary L² , proving the displayed direct sum.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Theorem H3 · The limit-of-discrete-series identification
text: H3 Theorem H3. The limit-of-discrete-series identification [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] The two summands in H2 are the two spinor limits of discrete series of Spin₀ (4,1) ≃ Sp (1,1) . Their minimal compact types are V₀ ⊠ V₁ and V₁ ⊠ V₀ . H1–H2 identify the normalized spinor boundary representation and its two irreducible summands, distinguished by their half-spin minimal compact types. Camporesi–Pedon, printed pp. 250–252, Theorem 3.2 and its proof, identify these half-spin endpoint representations as limits of discrete series, using the standard classification. Liu–Zhang, printed p. 2996 immediately after Theorem 3.11, identify the regular ℋ₁ model as their limit π₁ . This proves the classification using those published representation-theoretic results; the classification theorem itself is an external input, while H1–H2 supply the explicit realization and splitting.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Proposition H4 · Failure of square-integrability and the Hardy replacement
text: H4 Proposition H4. Failure of square-integrability and the Hardy replacement There is no nonzero regular function with finite ball integral ∫_(B)|h|²s^(− 1)dv . The nonzero matrix coefficient between constant vectors of ℋ₊ is in L^(p)(G) exactly for p > 2 (among positive p ); in particular the representation is not discrete series. Write s = 1 − |q|² . The lift of a constant vector on the ball has size s^(3/2) on the standard section, whereas G/K has invariant measure proportional to s^(− 4)dv . Averaging the absolute p th power of its nonzero constant-vector matrix coefficient over the compact fibre gives a positive constant times ∫_(B)s^(3p/2 − 4)dv. This is finite exactly when p > 2 . In particular these coefficients are not in L²(G) . The attempted ball norm with density s^(− 1)dv also has no nonzero regular vectors, by monotonicity of spherical square means. The Hardy condition provides the correct nonzero Hilbert realization. For the first assertion, spherical square means M(r) are nondecreasing, either by the expansion in H1 or subharmonicity. If h ≠ 0 , then M(r₀) > 0 at some radius and ∫_(r₀)¹M(r)(r³)/(1 − r²)dr = ∞. For the coefficient, harmonic mean values identify pairing with a constant with evaluation at zero. On the section the lift is s^(3/2)v . Compact integration of | ⟨ τ₁(k)^(− 1)v,w ⟩ |^(p) is a fixed strictly positive constant for nonzero v,w . The remaining radial integral converges exactly when 3p/2 − 4 > − 1 , namely p > 2 .

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Proposition H5 · Kelvin inversion and exterior regular functions
text: H5 Proposition H5. Kelvin inversion and exterior regular functions Let ℋₑₓₜ consist of regular functions on |q| > 1 with finite norm ‖u‖ₑₓₜ² = sup_(R > 1) R⁶∫_(S³)|u(Rω)|²dσ(ω). The transform (Kh)(q) = |q|^(− 2)q^(− 1)h(q^(− 1)) is an isometric bijection ℋ₊ → ℋₑₓₜ . Its boundary trace is the involution C in H2, so the exterior boundary space is ℋ_(−) . These exterior functions decay as O(|q|^(− 3)) at infinity. Put G(q) = q̄/|q|⁴ . Product and chain rules, with DₗG = 0 , give Dₗ(G(q)h(q^(− 1))) = − (q)/(|q|⁶)(Dₗh)(q^(− 1)). To verify the coefficient in the chain rule, use d(q^(− 1))v = − q^(− 1)vq^(− 1) . For the real orthonormal basis e_(μ) = 1,i,j,k , the adjoint of v ↦ q̄vq̄ is v ↦ qvq . Thus the coefficient of ∂_(ν)h in the product derivative is − qe_(ν)/|q|⁶ , proving the identity. It proves regularity on the punctured domain. Also G(q)G(q^(− 1)) = 1 , so K² = 1 where defined. For q = Rω , |G(q)| = R^(− 3) and q^(− 1) = R^(− 1)ω̄ . Therefore R⁶∫_(S³)|(Kh)(Rω)|²dσ = ∫_(S³)|h(R^(− 1)ω)|²dσ. Taking suprema proves the isometry. Conversely the same identity sends an exterior function to a regular function on the punctured ball with bounded spherical square means near zero. Each harmonic component's spherical expansion has no singular term under this bound, so the singularity is removable. Its extension is regular and in ℋ₊ . At infinity the image of an interior function is O(R^(− 3)) since the interior function is bounded near zero. Taking the L² boundary limit gives (Ch)(ω) = ω̄h(ω̄) .

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Boundary values and the conformal action
text: Boundary values and the conformal action Put B = {q ∈ ℍ : |q| < 1} . Use q = t + ix + jy + kz , Dₗ = ∂ₜ + i∂ₓ + j∂_(y) + k∂_(z) , and right complex scalars in ℍ . Let dσ be probability area on S³ . Definition H-D1. The Regular Hardy Space The Fueter Hardy space consists of the smooth functions in ℋ₊ = {h : B → ℍ : Dₗh = 0, ‖h‖² = sup_(0 < r < 1) ∫_(S³)|h(rω)|²dσ(ω) < ∞}. For γ^(− 1) = (a, b; c, d) , set , q^(′) = (aq + b)(cq + d)^(− 1), J = cq + d, (Π (γ)h)(q) = |J|^(− 2)J^(− 1)h(q^(′))., (H1) The action and boundary trace are established in H1. Theorem H1. An irreducible unitary representation on ordinary regular functions [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] The Hardy boundary trace identifies ℋ₊ isometrically with a closed invariant subspace of L²(S³,ℍ) . Its action is strongly continuous, unitary and irreducible, with ℋ₊|_(K) = ⨁̂_(m ≥ 0)Vₘ ⊠ V_(m + 1). The central element − I acts by − 1 , so the representation does not descend to SO₀(4,1) .

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: The principal series at parameter zero
text: The principal series at parameter zero Let P = MAN be the stabilizer of 1 ∈ S³ , with M ≃ Sp (1) embedded diagonally in K , and write σ = V₁ . Normalize A by aₜ = (cosh (t/2), sinh (t/2); sinh (t/2), cosh (t/2)). We use normalized induction: its sections satisfy F(gmaₜn) = e^(− 3t/2)σ(m)^(− 1)F(g). Proposition H-D2. The Boundary Model of Normalized Induction [1, §3, pp. 249–250] The formula (H1) extends to a unitary representation on ℬ = L²(S³,ℍ) and realizes , I(σ,0) = Ind_(MAN)^(G) (σ ⊗ 1 ⊗ 1), (H3) with the normalized induction convention above. Theorem H2. The two Hardy summands of the spinor principal series [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] For σ = V₁ of M ≃ Sp(1) , normalized induction at parameter zero splits as I(σ,0) = ℋ₊⊕︎ [ˆ]ℋ_(−), ℋ_(−) = Cℋ₊, (Cf)(ω) = ω̄f(ω̄). Both summands are irreducible and inequivalent. The second has compact types ⨁_(m ≥ 0)V_(m + 1) ⊠ Vₘ . Theorem H3. The limit-of-discrete-series identification [1, Thm. 3.2]; [2, after Thm. 3.11] The two summands in H2 are the two spinor limits of discrete series of Spin₀ (4,1) ≃ Sp (1,1) . Their minimal compact types are V₀ ⊠ V₁ and V₁ ⊠ V₀ .

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: Integrability at the endpoint
text: Integrability at the endpoint Proposition H4. Failure of square-integrability and the Hardy replacement There is no nonzero regular function with finite ball integral ∫_(B)|h|²s^(− 1)dv . The nonzero matrix coefficient between constant vectors of ℋ₊ is in L^(p)(G) exactly for p > 2 (among positive p ); in particular the representation is not discrete series.

title: The Fueter Hardy space
heading: The exterior regular model
text: The exterior regular model Proposition H5. Kelvin inversion and exterior regular functions Let ℋₑₓₜ consist of regular functions on |q| > 1 with finite norm ‖u‖ₑₓₜ² = sup_(R > 1) R⁶∫_(S³)|u(Rω)|²dσ(ω). The transform (Kh)(q) = |q|^(− 2)q^(− 1)h(q^(− 1)) is an isometric bijection ℋ₊ → ℋₑₓₜ . Its boundary trace is the involution C in H2, so the exterior boundary space is ℋ_(−) . These exterior functions decay as O(|q|^(− 3)) at infinity. Discussion The splitting H2 is analogous to the positive and negative Hardy spaces for the weight-one endpoint of SL₂(ℝ) . The elliptic coefficients use the same Cauchy kernel, but varying a lattice gives an SL₄ action. A direct correspondence between these two representations remains open.
