heading: Proposition AS3 · Matching the half-space kernel to the ball model
text: AS3 Proposition AS3. Matching the half-space kernel to the ball model [2, §2, Def. 2.1] Use the same quaternion embedding ι in both models. Put C = (1)/(√(2))(1, 1; − 1, 1). It takes B to {z : Re z > 0} by q ↦ (q + 1)(1 − q)^(− 1) . For a half-space group element h = (A, B; Cₕ, Dₕ) define D_(∗)(h) = (1)/(2)(h1 + 1)(Cₕ + Dₕ), ωₙ(h) = |D_(∗)(h)|^(− 2)τₙ(ι(D_(∗)(h)^(− 1))). For a ball group element g with lower-right block d_(g) , , D_(∗)(CgC^(− 1)) = d_(g)., (3) Let n > 4 and let ℱ be a smooth bounded, left Λ -invariant half-space group function with right compact transformation ℱ(hk) = τₙ(ι(Cₖ + Dₖ))^(− 1)ℱ(h) and reproducing identity , ℱ(g) = c ∫ ωₙ(h^(− 1)g)ℱ(h) dh,, (4) with c and Haar measure normalized as in that identity. Then, for Γ = C^(− 1)Λ C , the function f(q) = s^(− (n + 2)/2)ℱ(Cσ(q)C^(− 1)) is regular and has exactly the automorphy law of AC-D1. The assertion applies after restricting an adelic form satisfying Murase–Narita's Definition 2.1 to a fixed finite component. One may restrict further to a torsion-free finite-index subgroup to obtain the torsion-free quotient convention. Conjugation by C changes the ball's form diag (1, − 1) to the half-space form (0, 1; 1, 0) up to sign. Direct multiplication shows that the sum of all four blocks of CgC^(− 1) is 2d_(g) . Since D_(∗)(h) = (1)/(2)(A + B + Cₕ + Dₕ), this proves (3), with quaternion multiplication in its displayed order. For g = diag (a,b) , the denominator at 1 of CgC^(− 1) is b . The compact type is therefore our right-hand factor Vₙ , with no change of the integer n . Write F(g) = ℱ(CgC^(− 1)) . Equation (3) turns (4) into F(g) = c∫_(G)|d_(h^(− 1)g)|^(− 2)τₙ(ι(d_(h^(− 1)g)^(− 1)))F(h) dh. After setting g = σ(q) and multiplying by s^(− (n + 2)/2) , the integrand is precisely πₙ(h)c_(F(h))(q) , the translated constant spinor with value F(h) . It is regular. Boundedness of F , the integrable Cartan estimate of AS1, and its derivative bounds on compact subsets of B justify differentiation under the integral. Hence f is regular. Right compact equivariance and left Γ invariance give the ball automorphy law by AC1. The resulting section is nonzero whenever this restricted group function is nonzero.

title: Theta Lifts and the Classical Weight-Two Dimension
heading: Corollary AS4 · Dimension on compact quotients
text: AS4 Corollary AS4. Dimension on compact quotients [1, (1), §2.2] Let X = Γ \ B be compact and connected, with Γ torsion-free. Then , dim_(ℂ) ℳ₂(Γ ) = b₂^(−)(X) = (χ(X))/(2) − 1 + b₁(X)., (5) Here b₂^(−) uses the orientation in AC8. For a finite cover Y → X of degree D , dim_(ℂ) ℳ₂(π₁Y) ≥ (Dχ(X))/(2) − 1. Thus covers of unbounded degree supply nonzero weight-two forms and unbounded dimensions. AC8 and Hodge theory identify the space with complex anti-self-dual harmonic two-forms. A real hyperbolic four-manifold has signature zero. Explicitly, for an orthonormal coframe its curvature matrix has entries Θᵢⱼ = Kθᵢ ∧ θⱼ , so tr (Θ ∧ Θ ) = 0 and the first Pontryagin form vanishes. The signature theorem gives b₂⁺ = b₂^(−) . Poincaré duality gives χ = 2 − 2b₁ + b₂ , proving (5). Finally χ(Y) = Dχ(X) , b₁(Y) ≥ 0 , and Chern–Gauss–Bonnet gives χ(X) > 0 for a compact hyperbolic four-manifold. This proves the bound and growth assertion. Such covers exist, for example along a separating tower in a cocompact arithmetic lattice.

title: Theta Lifts and the Classical Weight-Two Dimension
heading: Arakawa theta lifts from classical forms
text: Arakawa theta lifts from classical forms Discussion [2], takes an elliptic cusp form and an automorphic form on a definite quaternion algebra and constructs a vector-valued automorphic form on GSp(1,1) . Their Theorem 4.1 treats even n > 6 . Restricting to the isometry group and fixing the finite adelic component gives a form on an arithmetic ball quotient. The kernel calculation below identifies its real-place condition with our regular-spinor model. [3] proves that some such lifts are nonzero. Only its publisher abstract has been inspected here; no individual input pair has yet been reconstructed. An arbitrary pair of input forms need not have nonzero lift. Proposition AS3. Matching the half-space kernel to the ball model [2, §2, Def. 2.1] Use the same quaternion embedding ι in both models. Put C = (1)/(√(2))(1, 1; − 1, 1). It takes B to {z : Re z > 0} by q ↦ (q + 1)(1 − q)^(− 1) . For a half-space group element h = (A, B; Cₕ, Dₕ) define D_(∗)(h) = (1)/(2)(h1 + 1)(Cₕ + Dₕ), ωₙ(h) = |D_(∗)(h)|^(− 2)τₙ(ι(D_(∗)(h)^(− 1))). For a ball group element g with lower-right block d_(g) , , D_(∗)(CgC^(− 1)) = d_(g)., (3) Let n > 4 and let ℱ be a smooth bounded, left Λ -invariant half-space group function with right compact transformation ℱ(hk) = τₙ(ι(Cₖ + Dₖ))^(− 1)ℱ(h) and reproducing identity , ℱ(g) = c ∫ ωₙ(h^(− 1)g)ℱ(h) dh,, (4) with c and Haar measure normalized as in that identity. Then, for Γ = C^(− 1)Λ C , the function f(q) = s^(− (n + 2)/2)ℱ(Cσ(q)C^(− 1)) is regular and has exactly the automorphy law of AC-D1. The assertion applies after restricting an adelic form satisfying Murase–Narita's Definition 2.1 to a fixed finite component. One may restrict further to a torsion-free finite-index subgroup to obtain the torsion-free quotient convention. Discussion This identifies the theta-lift outputs with the present definition by a kernel computation, rather than by their compact types alone. The arithmetic construction and its cusp property remain external inputs from the cited literature. These lifts offer a promising route to Hecke eigenvalues, Fourier coefficients, and periods; a specific nonzero pair is a useful next example to work out.

title: Theta Lifts and the Classical Weight-Two Dimension
heading: The geometric supply at weight two
text: The geometric supply at weight two Corollary AS4. Dimension on compact quotients [1, (1), §2.2] Let X = Γ \ B be compact and connected, with Γ torsion-free. Then , dim_(ℂ) ℳ₂(Γ ) = b₂^(−)(X) = (χ(X))/(2) − 1 + b₁(X)., (5) Here b₂^(−) uses the orientation in AC8. For a finite cover Y → X of degree D , dim_(ℂ) ℳ₂(π₁Y) ≥ (Dχ(X))/(2) − 1. Thus covers of unbounded degree supply nonzero weight-two forms and unbounded dimensions. Discussion The three constructions serve different purposes. Poincaré series prove existence and give explicit convergent sums. Theta lifts supply arithmetic structure. At weight two, topology measures the space exactly on compact quotients. The cuspidal correspondence and dimension formula identify the parabolic image using both chiralities and give explicit principal-level dimensions for n ≥ 5 . The weight-fourteen example specifies a congruence lattice, proves nonvanishing by an explicit tail estimate, and writes its (a,a) period as a surface Mellin integral. Low-weight noncompact dimensions remain a further question.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Overview
text: Expository A cusp-adapted matrix model for Sp(1,r), its Cayley transform, and the quaternionic Heisenberg boundary. Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains Discussion The half-space model puts a chosen cusp at infinity. Its stabilizer acts by translations, rotations and dilations, so growth, constant terms and Mellin integration can be written directly in cusp coordinates. In quaternionic dimension one the domain is {z ∈ ℍ : Re z > 0} . In every higher quaternionic dimension there is a corresponding Siegel domain, isomorphic to the ball for the same group Sp(1,r) . The dimension is denoted by r here; spinor weight will be denoted by k . This keeps the two parameters separate. Matrices act on columns on the left, and projective coordinates are normalized by multiplication by the inverse of the last coordinate on the right.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Proposition QH1 · The Action and Height Factor
text: QH1 Proposition QH1. The Action and Height Factor [2, §§3, 6] The projective action above is defined throughout ℋᵣ . Its denominator and height satisfy , j(g₁g₂,z) = j(g₁,g₂z)j(g₂,z), Y(gz) = (Y(z))/(|j(g,z)|²)., (Q1) A vector (η₀,η^(′),0) has Hermitian value ‖η^(′)‖² ≥ 0 . Since gv has negative value, its last coordinate cannot vanish. Multiplying gv on the right by j^(− 1) gives its normalized representative. A quaternionic Hermitian value scales by |j|^(− 2) under this multiplication, proving the height formula. Apply this normalization first to g₂v and then to g₁(g₂v) to obtain the denominator identity, with the displayed multiplication order. It also proves the action law.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Proposition QH2 · Cayley Coordinates in Every Dimension
text: QH2 Proposition QH2. Cayley Coordinates in Every Dimension [2, §§3, 6] Let Bᵣ = {(q^(′),qᵣ) ∈ ℍ^(r − 1) × ℍ : ‖q^(′)‖² + |qᵣ|² < 1} and J_(B) = diag (Iᵣ, − 1) . Define the real matrix Cᵣ by Cᵣ(q^(′); qᵣ; 1) = ((qᵣ + 1)/√(2); q^(′); (1 − qᵣ)/√(2)). Then Cᵣ^(∗)JᵣCᵣ = J_(B) , and conjugation by Cᵣ identifies the ball group preserving J_(B) with Gᵣ . The induced bijection is , w = (1 + qᵣ)(1 − qᵣ)^(− 1), ζ = √(2) q^(′)(1 − qᵣ)^(− 1)., (Q2) Its inverse and height are , qᵣ = (w − 1)(w + 1)^(− 1), q^(′) = √(2) ζ(w + 1)^(− 1), Y = (1 − ‖q^(′)‖² − |qᵣ|²)/(|1 − qᵣ|²)., (Q3) The real two-by-two change in the last ball coordinate and the homogenizing coordinate takes their diagonal form to the off-diagonal block of Jᵣ ; the other coordinates are unchanged. This proves the matrix identity. Normalize the displayed vector by its last coordinate to obtain Q2. Quaternionic norm multiplicativity and Re ((1 + qᵣ)(1 − qᵣ)^(− 1)) = (1 − |qᵣ|²)/(|1 − qᵣ|²) give Q3. The proposed inverse follows by solving Q2, and the height identity shows that it maps precisely ℋᵣ onto Bᵣ . Conjugating a matrix preserving J_(B) now gives a matrix preserving Jᵣ .

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Proposition QH3 · The Quaternionic Heisenberg Translations
text: QH3 Proposition QH3. The Quaternionic Heisenberg Translations [2, §§3, 6] For v ∈ ℍ^(r − 1) and t ∈ Im ℍ , put n(v,t) = (1, v^(∗), ‖v‖²/2 + t; 0, I_(r − 1), v; 0, 0, 1), a_(λ) = diag (λ,I_(r − 1),λ^(− 1)) (λ > 0). These matrices belong to Gᵣ and fix infinity. Their actions and multiplication law are , n(v,t)(w,ζ) = (w + v^(∗)ζ + ‖v‖²/2 + t, ζ + v),, (Q4) , n(v,t)n(v^(′),t^(′)) = n(v + v^(′),t + t^(′) + Im (v^(∗)v^(′))),, (Q5) , a_(λ)(w,ζ) = (λ²w,λζ), Y(n(v,t)z) = Y(z), Y(a_(λ)z) = λ²Y(z)., (Q6) For r = 1 , N₁ = {n(0,t)} is the additive group Im ℍ . For r > 1 , the group Nᵣ = {n(v,t)} is two-step nilpotent, with center {n(0,t)} and commutator , [n(v,t),n(v^(′),t^(′))] = n(0,2 Im (v^(∗)v^(′)))., (Q7) Multiplication gives n(v,t)^(∗)Jᵣn(v,t) = Jᵣ , using t + t̄ = 0 ; the diagonal identity for a_(λ) follows immediately. The last denominator of n(v,t) is one, yielding Q4. In the top-right entry of a product, separate v^(∗)v^(′) into real and imaginary parts. Its real part combines with ‖v‖²/2 + ‖v^(′)‖²/2 to give ‖v + v^(′)‖²/2 , proving Q5. Inverses are n( − v, − t) , so Q7 follows. At r > 1 , if v ≠ 0 , one can choose v^(′) with Im (v^(∗)v^(′)) ≠ 0 , which identifies the center. Q6 follows either directly or from Q1.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Definition QH-D3 · The Schmid Operator
text: QH-D3 Definition QH-D3. The Schmid Operator For k ≥ 1 , the Schmid operator is Dₖ = pr_(Sym^(k − 1) S ⊗ U) ∘ ∇ .

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Proposition QH4 · Weight and Cohomological Degree
text: QH4 Proposition QH4. Weight and Cohomological Degree [1, §§1.5, 2.4–2.5] Let r ≥ 1 and k ≥ 2r , and put m = k − 2r . Let πₖ be the quaternionic discrete series of Gᵣ whose minimal compact type is Sym^(k) S , trivial on Sp(r) . Put Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ^(2r + 2) , the symmetric power of the standard complex representation. Then dim_(ℂ) H^(j)(gᵣ,Kᵣ;(πₖ)_(Kᵣ) ⊗ Eₘ) = {1, j = 2r,; 0, j ≠ 2r. Here (πₖ)_(Kᵣ) is the module of compact-finite smooth vectors, and relative Lie algebra cohomology is defined by the complex in CP-D3. Order the compact Cartan coordinates with the distinguished Sp(1) coordinate first. The coefficient highest weight is λ = (m,0,…,0) , and the half-sums of positive roots are ρ = (r + 1,r,r − 1,…,1), ρ_(c) = (1,r,r − 1,…,1). The parameter λ + ρ is regular for m ≥ 0 . Its minimal compact weight is λ + 2(ρ − ρ_(c)) = (k,0,…,0) , identifying the specified member of the discrete-series packet. Grobner §1.5 gives one-dimensional discrete-series cohomology in the middle degree when the infinitesimal characters match; §2.4 gives that degree as 2r , and §2.5 matches the quaternionic minimal type and recalls its existence for k ≥ 2r . The stronger k > 4r assumption used for integrable matrix coefficients in his later multiplicity calculation is not needed for this relative-cohomology assertion. For r = 1 , CP4 supplies the compact-type calculation directly.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: A Matrix Realization Adapted to Infinity
text: A Matrix Realization Adapted to Infinity For an integer r ≥ 1 , put Jᵣ = (0, 0, − 1; 0, I_(r − 1), 0; − 1, 0, 0), Gᵣ = {g ∈ GL_(r + 1) (ℍ) : g^(∗)Jᵣg = Jᵣ}, where g^(∗) is quaternionic conjugate transpose. At r = 1 the middle row and column are absent. For a quaternionic column ζ , put ‖ζ‖² = ζ^(∗)ζ = ∑ⱼ|ζⱼ|² . For r ≥ 1 , use the quaternionic Siegel model and height function ℋᵣ = {(w,ζ) ∈ ℍ × ℍ^(r − 1) : 2 Re w > ‖ζ‖²}, Y(w,ζ) = Re w − (1)/(2)‖ζ‖². The projective model uses the right quaternionic line through v(w,ζ) = (w; ζ; 1), v^(∗)Jᵣv = − 2Y(w,ζ). For g ∈ Gᵣ , write gv = (η₀,η^(′),j)^(t) and define g ⋅ (w,ζ) = (η₀j^(− 1),η^(′)j^(− 1)), j(g,(w,ζ)) = j. The identity v^(∗)Jᵣv = − 2Y follows by multiplication, so these are precisely the negative lines with last coordinate nonzero. An isotropic line with last coordinate zero has ζ^(∗)ζ = 0 , hence ζ = 0 . Thus the boundary consists of Y = 0 and the point ∞ = [1 : 0 : ⋯ : 0] . The action is well-defined by QH1. Proposition QH1. The Action and Height Factor [2, §§3, 6] The projective action above is defined throughout ℋᵣ . Its denominator and height satisfy , j(g₁g₂,z) = j(g₁,g₂z)j(g₂,z), Y(gz) = (Y(z))/(|j(g,z)|²)., (Q1)

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: The Ball and the Same Real Group
text: The Ball and the Same Real Group Proposition QH2. Cayley Coordinates in Every Dimension [2, §§3, 6] Let Bᵣ = {(q^(′),qᵣ) ∈ ℍ^(r − 1) × ℍ : ‖q^(′)‖² + |qᵣ|² < 1} and J_(B) = diag (Iᵣ, − 1) . Define the real matrix Cᵣ by Cᵣ(q^(′); qᵣ; 1) = ((qᵣ + 1)/√(2); q^(′); (1 − qᵣ)/√(2)). Then Cᵣ^(∗)JᵣCᵣ = J_(B) , and conjugation by Cᵣ identifies the ball group preserving J_(B) with Gᵣ . The induced bijection is , w = (1 + qᵣ)(1 − qᵣ)^(− 1), ζ = √(2) q^(′)(1 − qᵣ)^(− 1)., (Q2) Its inverse and height are , qᵣ = (w − 1)(w + 1)^(− 1), q^(′) = √(2) ζ(w + 1)^(− 1), Y = (1 − ‖q^(′)‖² − |qᵣ|²)/(|1 − qᵣ|²)., (Q3) Discussion The signatures (r,1) and (1,r) describe isomorphic groups: multiplying the defining form by − 1 does not change its isometry group. Thus Gᵣ is a realization of the family written Sp(1,r) in this wiki. The Cayley transform changes the matrix basis and domain, not the real form of the group. The distinction matters arithmetically. A rational group, its lattice, and its coefficient representations must be transported together under the change of basis. A real coordinate change alone does not make every new matrix entry rational, nor does it preserve an entrywise integral-level condition verbatim. Congruence and Hecke correspondences refer to the transported rational structure.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Translations, Dilations and Cusp Cross-Sections
text: Translations, Dilations and Cusp Cross-Sections Proposition QH3. The Quaternionic Heisenberg Translations [2, §§3, 6] For v ∈ ℍ^(r − 1) and t ∈ Im ℍ , put n(v,t) = (1, v^(∗), ‖v‖²/2 + t; 0, I_(r − 1), v; 0, 0, 1), a_(λ) = diag (λ,I_(r − 1),λ^(− 1)) (λ > 0). These matrices belong to Gᵣ and fix infinity. Their actions and multiplication law are , n(v,t)(w,ζ) = (w + v^(∗)ζ + ‖v‖²/2 + t, ζ + v),, (Q4) , n(v,t)n(v^(′),t^(′)) = n(v + v^(′),t + t^(′) + Im (v^(∗)v^(′))),, (Q5) , a_(λ)(w,ζ) = (λ²w,λζ), Y(n(v,t)z) = Y(z), Y(a_(λ)z) = λ²Y(z)., (Q6) For r = 1 , N₁ = {n(0,t)} is the additive group Im ℍ . For r > 1 , the group Nᵣ = {n(v,t)} is two-step nilpotent, with center {n(0,t)} and commutator , [n(v,t),n(v^(′),t^(′))] = n(0,2 Im (v^(∗)v^(′)))., (Q7) Discussion Every point has unique coordinates ζ = v, w = ‖v‖²/2 + t + y, y > 0, so ℋᵣ = Nᵣ × ℝ_(> 0) as a manifold. A cusp region is described by large y , with the Nᵣ -coordinate taken modulo a lattice and, possibly, a finite holonomy group. The geometry and normalization agree with the Siegel and horospherical models discussed in [2, §§3, 6], after accounting for their factor of two in the central and height coordinates. At r = 1 , a cusp cross-section is covered by a three-torus. At r > 1 , it is covered by a compact quotient of the quaternionic Heisenberg group. Functions on that quotient have noncommutative Fourier analysis: characters describe the part trivial on the center, while nonzero central frequencies require additional representations. The rank-three exponential series used for the one-variable Mellin construction belongs specifically to r = 1 .

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: The One-Variable Model
text: The One-Variable Model At r = 1 write ℋ = {z = y + x₁i + x₂j + x₃k : y > 0}, G = {g = (a, b; c, d) : g^(∗)(0, 1; 1, 0)g = (0, 1; 1, 0)}. Its action, denominator and metric are gz = (az + b)(cz + d)^(− 1), J(g,z) = cz + d, ds² = (dy² + dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃²)/(4y²). Set nₓ = (1, x; 0, 1), a_(y) = (√(y), 0; 0, 1/√(y)), W = (0, 1; 1, 0), C = (1)/(√(2))(1, 1; − 1, 1). For x ∈ Im ℍ , direct substitution gives nₓa_(y) ⋅ 1 = y + x , Wz = z^(− 1) , and QH2 carries the stabilizer of the ball origin to the maximal compact subgroup K = Stab_(G) (1) = C{diag (u,v) : |u| = |v| = 1}C^(− 1). For k ∈ K , put σ(k) = J(k,1) . If k = C diag (u,v)C^(− 1) , multiplication gives c = (v − u)/2 and d = (u + v)/2 , hence σ(k) = c + d = v . Discussion This is a real four-dimensional half-space. The word “half-plane” is an analogy with the complex upper half-plane; it does not reduce the quaternionic variable to two real coordinates. Positive real part is convenient because the three imaginary coordinates become the translation variables. The displayed metric has curvature − 4 and is the image of |dq|²/(1 − |q|²)² on the ball.

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Which Parts of the Classical Formulation Generalize?
text: Which Parts of the Classical Formulation Generalize? Discussion The bounded and unbounded models for the three relevant families are: Family Bounded model Unbounded model SU(1,r) Complex r -ball Complex rank-one Siegel domain Sp(1,r) Quaternionic r -ball Quaternionic Siegel domain ℋᵣ Sp₂ᵣ(ℝ) Bounded Siegel disk Complex symmetric matrices with positive-definite imaginary part In complex dimension one, SU(1,1) is isomorphic to SL₂(ℝ) ; U (1,1) has an additional central circle. The higher-dimensional complex ball and the matrix Siegel upper half-space are different symmetric spaces. Both have unbounded realizations, so passing to half-space coordinates does not select the real symplectic family. For quaternionic automorphic theory, a uniform formulation begins with Gᵣ , its maximal compact subgroup Kᵣ ≃ Sp(r) × Sp(1) , a homogeneous coefficient bundle, and the cusp constant term. The model of the symmetric space supplies coordinates for these objects. The one-variable article below uses the explicit flat Fueter equation after its scalar frame change; in higher dimensions the invariant Schmid operator retains the connection terms. Let Γ ⊂ Gᵣ be a congruence lattice in a rational-rank-one rational form. Set o = (1,0) ∈ ℋᵣ , Kᵣ = Stab_(Gᵣ) (o) , and let gᵣ = kᵣ ⊕︎ pᵣ be the Cartan decomposition of this symmetric pair. Let S = ℂ² be the standard representation of the distinguished Sp(1) factor of Kᵣ , let U = ℂ^(2r) be the standard representation of Sp(r) , and let Vₖ = Sym^(k) S with the other factor acting trivially. Smooth Γ -invariant sections of Gᵣ×_(Kᵣ)Vₖ are represented by smooth functions F : Gᵣ → Vₖ satisfying F(gk₀) = τₖ(k₀)^(− 1)F(g), F(γg) = F(g). Use the canonical homogeneous connection induced by the kᵣ component of g^(− 1)dg . The complex cotangent representation at o is Tₒ^(∗)ℋᵣ ⊗ ℂ ≃ S ⊗ U . The projection below uses the Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of Sym^(k) S ⊗ S . Vₖ ⊗ S ⊗ U ≃ (Sym^(k + 1) S ⊕︎ Sym^(k − 1) S) ⊗ U (k ≥ 1). Definition QH-D3. The Schmid Operator For k ≥ 1 , the Schmid operator is Dₖ = pr_(Sym^(k − 1) S ⊗ U) ∘ ∇ .

title: Quaternionic Half-Space and Siegel Domains
heading: Automorphic Conditions
text: Automorphic Conditions The cusp condition is ∫_((Γ ∩ N_(ξ)) \ N_(ξ))F(ug) du = 0 for every rational cusp ξ and every g ∈ Gᵣ, where the quotient Haar measure has total mass one. Moderate growth and central finiteness are defined as in CP-D0, using the Euclidean norm on ℍ^(r + 1) . Discussion The connection in QH-D3 is part of the operator. It is carried along by a change of group realization, so no coordinate change requires treating a moving section as flat. The degree and weight dictionary is stated in QH4 below. The explicit degree-two construction and its Mellin periods are developed for r = 1 in Cusp forms, Mellin transforms and parabolic cohomology. Proposition QH4. Weight and Cohomological Degree [1, §§1.5, 2.4–2.5] Let r ≥ 1 and k ≥ 2r , and put m = k − 2r . Let πₖ be the quaternionic discrete series of Gᵣ whose minimal compact type is Sym^(k) S , trivial on Sp(r) . Put Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ^(2r + 2) , the symmetric power of the standard complex representation. Then dim_(ℂ) H^(j)(gᵣ,Kᵣ;(πₖ)_(Kᵣ) ⊗ Eₘ) = {1, j = 2r,; 0, j ≠ 2r. Here (πₖ)_(Kᵣ) is the module of compact-finite smooth vectors, and relative Lie algebra cohomology is defined by the complex in CP-D3.
