title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Lemma CP4 · One Cohomology Generator per Discrete-Series Copy
text: CP4 Lemma CP4. One Cohomology Generator per Discrete-Series Copy [6, Thm. 7.1] Let n ≥ 2 , m = n − 2 , and let πₙ^(±) be the two reflected discrete series. Then , dim C^(j)(g,K;πₙ^(±) ⊗ Eₘ) = {1, j = 2,; 0, j ≠ 2. , (10) The unique cochain in degree two is, up to a nonzero scalar, the fiber map defining Ω^(±) . Thus it generates relative Lie algebra cohomology in degree two. Write Vₐ ⊠ V_(b) for a representation of K = Sp(1) × Sp(1) . The relevant decompositions are πₙ^(−)|_(K) = ⨁_(r ≥ 0)Vᵣ ⊠ V_(r + n), Eₘ|_(K) = ⨁_(a = 0)^(m)Vₐ ⊠ V_(m − a), Λ⁰p_(ℂ) ≃ Λ⁴p_(ℂ) ≃ V₀ ⊠ V₀, Λ¹p_(ℂ) ≃ Λ³p_(ℂ) ≃ V₁ ⊠ V₁, Λ²p_(ℂ) = (V₂ ⊠ V₀) ⊕︎ (V₀ ⊠ V₂). In the right tensor factor V_(r + n) ⊗ V_(m − a) , the smallest degree is r + a + 2 . Consequently degrees zero, one, three, and four have no cochains, and the V₂ ⊠ V₀ part in degree two contributes none. The V₀ ⊠ V₂ part forces r = a = 0 ; Vₙ ⊗ V_(n − 2) contains V₂ once. This proves (10) by the Clebsch–Gordan formula. The explicit fiber map is nonzero and equivariant by AC3, so it spans that line. There are no incoming or outgoing cochains. Reflection proves the other case.

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Theorem CP5 · The Degree-Two Cuspidal and Parabolic Correspondence
text: CP5 Theorem CP5. The Degree-Two Cuspidal and Parabolic Correspondence [6, Thm. 7.1]; [11, Thm. 4.3]; [3, Prop. 4.4(i), Prop. 5.4]; [9, App. A, pp. 29–30] Let G/ℚ be a simply connected semisimple group with G(ℝ) ≃ Sp(1,1) and ℚ -rank one, and let Γ be a torsion-free congruence lattice in G . Put X = Γ \ ℋ . For every integer n ≥ 2 , take the complex algebraic coefficient representation Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ , m = n − 2 , with its flat bundle and the transported positive homogeneous metric h^(ℋ) of CP-H1. Then the explicit period construction gives a complex-linear isomorphism , Sₙ^(−)(Γ ) ⊕︎ Sₙ⁺(Γ ) → [∼ []] Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ), , (11) (f_(−),f₊) ⟼ [Ω_(f_(−)) + Ω_(f₊)⁺]. Inside ordinary complex cohomology, Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ) = H_(!)²(X,ℰₘ) = H_(cusp)²(Γ ,Eₘ). With the spectral notation above, , H²(g,K;(Lᵣₑₛ²(Γ \ G))_(K)^(∞) ⊗ Eₘ) = 0., (11a) The restriction map in (6) induces an injection , H²(Γ ,Eₘ)/H_(cusp)²(Γ ,Eₘ) ↪ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),Eₘ)., (11c) The residual spectrum cannot contribute in degree two. The finite-coefficient harmonic spectral theorem identifies the space ℋ₍₂₎²(X,ℰₘ) with , ⨁_(π ⊂ L_(disc)²(Γ \ G))M_(Γ)(π) ⊗ H²(g,K;π_(K) ⊗ Eₘ),, (11b) where M_(Γ)(π) is the multiplicity space. The sum contributing to this degree is finite. This is the Borel–Garland result recorded in Borel–Casselman, Proposition 4.4(i), with its finite-coefficient scope explicitly recalled in Nair–Rai, Appendix A. It is a theorem about square-integrable harmonic forms, not an identification of arbitrary ordinary cohomology with L² cohomology. No continuous-spectrum harmonic term is omitted by (11b). Grobner's Theorem 7.1 says that only the two cohomological discrete series contribute in degree two. CP4 identifies them with πₙ^(±) . The other possible unitary cohomological representations have cohomology only in degrees 0,4 or 1,3 . In particular this remains true for the trivial coefficient system n = 2 . Every discrete series is tempered. Wallach's Theorem 4.3 says that a tempered (g,K) -module mapping to square-integrable automorphic forms has cuspidal image. It therefore places every occurrence of πₙ^(±) in L_(cusp)² , not in the residual spectrum. This proves (11a) and identifies (11b) with cuspidal degree-two cohomology. This spectral exclusion is independent of the direct constant-term argument in CP1. Interior classes have the required harmonic representatives. Let [α] ∈ H_(!)² , choosing α ∈ Ω_(c)²(X,ℰₘ) with d_(∇)α = 0 . Give X the complete half-space metric and the bundle its metric h^(ℋ) from CP-H1. Let dⱼ be the closed L² extension of d_(∇) in degree j , with Hilbert adjoint dⱼ^(∗) . The Hilbert-complex decomposition is L²Ω² = ℋ₍₂₎² ⊕︎ [ˆ] overline(im d₁) ⊕︎ [ˆ] overline(im d₂^(∗)), ℋ₍₂₎² = ker d₂ ∩ ker d₁^(∗). Since d₂α = 0 , α is orthogonal to im d₂^(∗) , so its last component vanishes. Its harmonic projection η is smooth by elliptic regularity. Completeness permits approximation in the graph norm by compactly supported smooth forms: scalar cutoffs with gradients tending to zero commute with d_(∇) up to exterior multiplication by their differential. Consequently there exist uⱼ ∈ Ω_(c)¹(X,ℰₘ) with d_(∇)uⱼ ⟶ α − η in L². Take any β ∈ Ω_(c)²(X,ℰₘ^(∨)) with d_(∇^(∨))β = 0 , where ℰₘ^(∨) is the dual flat bundle. Parallel evaluation and Stokes give ∫_(X)ev (d_(∇)uⱼ ∧ β) = ∫_(X)d ev (uⱼ ∧ β) = 0. On the compact support of β , the dual metric and Cauchy–Schwarz give a constant C_(β) with |∫_(X)ev ((α − η − d_(∇)uⱼ) ∧ β)| ≤ C_(β)‖α − η − d_(∇)uⱼ‖_(L²) ⟶ 0. Thus ∫_(X)ev ((α − η) ∧ β) = 0 for every such β . Poincaré duality with local coefficients makes the pairing H²(X,ℰₘ) × H_(c)²(X,ℰₘ^(∨)) ⟶ ℂ, ([ω],[β]) ⟼ ∫_(X)ev (ω ∧ β) nondegenerate: X is oriented, has real dimension four, and has a finite compact core. Applying it to the smooth closed form α − η proves [α] = [η] in ordinary cohomology. This is the step converting the L² limit into an equality of ordinary classes; it does not assume that the space of smooth exact forms is L² -closed. The spectral identification (11b) and its geometric comparison identify [η] with the image under κ₂ of a cuspidal cohomology class. Thus H_(!)² ⊆ im (ℋ₍₂₎² → H²) = H_(cusp)². Conversely CP4 identifies each cuspidal cohomological generator with one of the explicit two-forms, and CP3 and reflection show that their restrictions to cusp stabilizers are exact. Consequently H_(cusp)² ⊆ Hₚₐᵣ² = H_(!)² by CP2. These inclusions prove the equality of the three subspaces. Identifying the explicit period map. In each occurrence of πₙ^(−) , the calculation in CP4 shows that the degree-two relative cochain is built entirely from the minimal compact type V₀ ⊠ Vₙ . Its fiber map is precisely the nonzero K -equivariant map λ^(−) : Vₙ ⟶ Λ²p_(ℂ)^(∗) ⊗ Eₘ defined by AC3. Since Vₙ is irreducible, λ^(−) is injective. Thus a harmonic form in this summand has homogeneous-frame coefficients λ^(−)F(g) , with a unique Vₙ -valued function F . Equivariance of λ^(−) gives the equivariance law of the group lift, so F determines a half-space spinor f . Closedness of the form is equivalent to regularity of f by AC3. Its scalar coefficients belong to the cuspidal automorphic module; applying the fixed inverse of λ^(−) on its image preserves zero constant terms, moderate growth, and central finiteness. Hence f ∈ Sₙ^(−)(Γ ) . Reflection gives the same reconstruction for πₙ⁺ . Conversely CP1 and AC6 send each cusp spinor to a square-integrable harmonic form, and CP4 identifies that map with this same fiber map in each cuspidal copy. The two chiralities lie in distinct Hodge-star eigenspaces, so their images have zero intersection. It follows that their sum identifies Sₙ^(−) ⊕︎ Sₙ⁺ with ℋ₍₂₎² . The map from this harmonic space to ordinary cohomology is the injective cuspidal comparison κ₂ on the spectral summands. The preceding interior-class argument identifies its image with Hₚₐᵣ² . Their composite is exactly (f_(−),f₊) ↦ [Ω_(f_(−)) + Ω_(f₊)⁺] , proving both injectivity and surjectivity in (11). Finally ker (res) = Hₚₐᵣ² = H_(cusp)² . Thus res factors through the quotient by H_(cusp)² , and the induced map has zero kernel. This proves (11c).

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Corollary CP6 · Dimensions at Principal Congruence Level
text: CP6 Corollary CP6. Dimensions at Principal Congruence Level [6, Prop. 7.1, §7.2]; [1, Thm. 2]; [2, Prop. 5.4] Let D/ℚ be a definite quaternion algebra with discriminant d(D) , and fix a maximal order O . Define the ball realization G_(B) by G_(B)(ℚ) = {g ∈ GL₂ (D) : g^(∗)diag (1, − 1)g = diag (1, − 1)}, where g^(∗) is the quaternionic conjugate transpose. Fix D⊗_(ℚ)ℝ ≃ ℍ , and identify the half-space real group by g ↦ CgC^(− 1) , transporting the rational structure. For an integer N ≥ 3 , let Γ (N) = C{g = (gᵢⱼ) ∈ G_(B)(ℚ) : gᵢⱼ − δᵢⱼ ∈ NO}C^(− 1), N ≥ 3. Write h = h(Γ (N)) for its number of cusps. For every integer n ≥ 5 , , dim_(ℂ) Sₙ^(−)(Γ (N)) = dim_(ℂ) Sₙ⁺(Γ (N)) = h[(N³(n³ − n))/(1440)∏_(p|d(D))(p² + 1) − 1]., (12) For the same N and n , dim_(ℂ) Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ (N),E_(n − 2)) = 2h[(N³(n³ − n))/(1440)∏_(p|d(D))(p² + 1) − 1]. The standard complex four-dimensional representation has highest weight μ₁ in Grobner's compact-Cartan coordinates. Thus E_(n − 2) has highest weight (n − 2)μ₁ , and his parameter ν is exactly n . His Proposition 7.1 gives the right-hand side of (12), with denominator 2⁵3²5 = 1440 , as the cuspidal multiplicity of A⁺(μ) for ν > 4 and N ≥ 3 . By CP4 this multiplicity equals the dimension of one of our spinor spaces. It is not multiplied by dim Vₙ = n + 1 : the space of equivariant maps from the minimal compact type into each discrete-series copy is one-dimensional. In the ball realization, the block-swap matrix W_(B) = (0, 1; 1, 0) normalizes the entrywise principal group: it changes the Hermitian form by a sign and preserves the entrywise congruence condition. Its half-space conjugate is CW_(B)C^(− 1) = D₀ , which exchanges the two discrete series, so their multiplicities agree. This removes any dependence on which sign is called plus in the source. Equation (11) gives the last assertion. The multiplicity formula is an external input, not a new derivation of the trace formula. Grobner's §7.2 writes it as formal degree times covolume minus h ; the unipotent contribution uses Arakawa (1984), Proposition 5.4.

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Proposition CP7 · A Number-Field Model for Parabolic Cohomology
text: CP7 Proposition CP7. A Number-Field Model for Parabolic Cohomology [8, 20.7–20.9] Let G/ℚ be a simply connected semisimple group of rational rank one with G(ℝ) ≃ Sp(1,1) , and let Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) be a torsion-free congruence lattice. Let n ≥ 2 and m = n − 2 . There exist a number field L ⊂ ℂ , an algebraic representation ρ_(m,L) : G_(L) → GL (E_(m,L)) , and an isomorphism , (E_(m,L),ρ_(m,L))⊗_(L)ℂ ≃ (Eₘ,Rₘ), Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴., (13) For every such choice define , H_(L) = ker (H²(Γ ,E_(m,L)) ⟶ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),E_(m,L)))., (14) Then H_(L) is finite-dimensional over L , and scalar extension induces an isomorphism , H_(L)⊗_(L)ℂ ≃ Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ)., (15) For m = 0 one may take L = ℚ . If m is odd, the complex representation Eₘ of G has no real model, and consequently (13) has no model over ℚ . Choose a finite extension L/ℚ splitting G . Such an extension exists: a splitting over ℚ̄ is specified by finitely many algebraic coefficients. The split group is of type C₂ and is simply connected, hence is isomorphic to Sp₄ over L . Its symmetric-power representation on Sym^(m) L⁴ has highest weight mω₁ , where ω₁ is the highest weight of the standard four-dimensional representation. Highest-weight classification identifies its complexification with Eₘ . Equivalently, Milne 20.7 descends this semisimple representation from ℂ to a splitting field. Fix one such identification in (13). For the quaternionic matrix group in CP6 this can be made explicit. Write D = (a,b)_(ℚ) with generators I² = a , J² = b , IJ = − JI and a,b < 0 . Over L = ℚ(√(a)) the matrices , I ⟼ (√(a), 0; 0, − √(a)), J ⟼ (0, b; 1, 0), (16) satisfy these relations and, together with the identity and their product, span M₂(L) . Thus they give a splitting D ⊗ L ≃ M₂(L) . Applying it to each entry of M₂(D) gives the four-dimensional representation over L ; take its m th symmetric power. After extension to ℂ , the two identifications of the split matrix algebra are conjugate, so this is isomorphic to the analytic block representation Rₘ . At m = 0 the representation is trivial and already defined over ℚ . For finiteness and (15), use the compact core X̄ and its boundary from CP2. They have finite CW structures, and their cellular cochains with the local system associated to E_(m,L) are finite-dimensional L -vector spaces. These complexes compute the cohomology groups in (14), because their universal covers are contractible. Tensoring with ℂ is exact, so it commutes with their cohomology and the kernel of boundary restriction. This proves both assertions. This construction uses cellular cochains over L ; de Rham forms enter only after scalar extension to ℂ . For the obstruction when m is odd, put J₀v = diag (ϵ,ϵ)v̄ , with ϵ as in AC-C1. Directly from the quaternionic block matrices, J₀R(g) = R(g)J₀ and J₀² = − 1 . Its induced antilinear map Jₘ on Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ satisfies Jₘ² = ( − 1)^(m) . This symmetric power is an irreducible complex G -representation. By Schur's lemma, any invertible equivariant antilinear map is cJₘ for some c ∈ ℂ^(×) . For odd m its square is − |c|² , never 1 . A real model would supply an equivariant antilinear involution, which is impossible.

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: The Condition on Group Cocycles
text: The Condition on Group Cocycles Put X = Γ \ ℋ , m = n − 2 , Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ , and ρ = Sym^(m) R . Let ℰₘ = Γ \ (ℋ × Eₘ) be the flat bundle for the action (z,v) ↦ (γz,ρ(γ)v) , with flat differential d_(∇) . For each rational cusp, put Γ_(ξ) = Γ ∩ P_(ξ) . For j ≥ 0 , write Ω^(j)(X,ℰₘ) for smooth bundle-valued j -forms and Ω_(c)^(j)(X,ℰₘ) for those with compact support; set both spaces to zero in degree − 1 . Define H^(j)(X,ℰₘ) = (ker (d_(∇) : Ω^(j) → Ω^(j + 1)))/(d_(∇)Ω^(j − 1)), H_(c)^(j)(X,ℰₘ) = (ker (d_(∇) : Ω_(c)^(j) → Ω_(c)^(j + 1)))/(d_(∇)Ω_(c)^(j − 1)). The inclusion of complexes induces j_(c) : H_(c)^(j)(X,ℰₘ) → H^(j)(X,ℰₘ) . Definition CP-D2. Interior and Parabolic Cohomology Interior cohomology is the subspace , H_(!)^(j)(X,ℰₘ) : = im j_(c) ⊆ H^(j)(X,ℰₘ)., (I) Parabolic cohomology is , Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ) = ker (H²(Γ ,Eₘ) ⟶ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),Eₘ))., (6) Identify H^(j)(Γ ,Eₘ) with H^(j)(X,ℰₘ) by the de Rham comparison for the contractible universal cover ℋ . [4, §§8, 15]; [5, Thm. I.7.5, §§III.1, III.8]. In inhomogeneous group-cochain notation, a two-cocycle c represents such a class exactly when, for every cusp, there is a one-cochain b_(ξ) : Γ_(ξ) → Eₘ such that , c(u,v) = ρ(u)b_(ξ)(v) − b_(ξ)(uv) + b_(ξ)(u), u,v ∈ Γ_(ξ). , (7) Indeed, membership in the kernel (6) says exactly that the restriction of c to each Γ_(ξ) is a coboundary. Formula (7) is the inhomogeneous differential of a one-cochain. Discussion The notation H_(!)² denotes the image of j_(c) in ordinary cohomology. A compactly supported closed form can be exact with a primitive that is not compactly supported, so the map j_(c) need not be injective. Its image is a different object from its domain. CP2 identifies this image with the parabolic subspace. The companion article Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support develops the topological comparison using the full stabilizers of geometric cusps, with a detailed proof of the relative-cohomology sequence and the cutoff construction. For a neat group, Γ_(ξ) ≃ ℤ³ ; in general it is virtually ℤ³ . In the classical surface case the cusp stabilizer is cyclic, and a degree-one cocycle becomes a coboundary there. Equation (7) is the corresponding degree-two condition. It does not ask the cocycle itself to vanish, and separate conditions on individual parabolic elements would be insufficient. Example. Why cyclic tests miss the condition Take n = 2 , so the coefficient representation is trivial, and let the cusp group be ℤ³ . The cocycle c(u,v) = u₁v₂ has nonzero alternating part, so its class in H²(ℤ³,ℂ) is nonzero. Its restriction to every cyclic subgroup is nevertheless a coboundary: on the subgroup generated by a , take b(ka) = − k(k − 1)a₁a₂/2 . In fact H²(ℤ,E) = 0 for every coefficient module E . Proposition CP2. Parabolic Cohomology Is Interior Cohomology [4, §§8, 15]; [5, Thm. I.7.5, §§III.1, III.8]; [7, Prop. 4.2.17, Cor. 4.2.18] Let G/ℚ be a simply connected semisimple group of rational rank one with G(ℝ) ≃ Sp(1,1) , and let Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) be a torsion-free congruence lattice. Put X = Γ \ ℋ and Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ , with m ≥ 0 . Then , Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ) = H_(!)²(X,ℰₘ) : = im (H_(c)²(X,ℰₘ) → H²(X,ℰₘ))., (8)

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: The Cohomological and Spectral Notation
text: The Cohomological and Spectral Notation Write g = k ⊕︎ p for the Cartan decomposition determined by K . Definition CP-D3. Relative Lie Algebra Cohomology For a (g_(ℂ),K) -module V , its relative cochain complex with coefficients Eₘ is C^(j)(g,K;V ⊗ Eₘ) = Hom_(K) (Λ^(j)p_(ℂ),V ⊗ Eₘ). The Lie algebra acts diagonally on V ⊗ Eₘ . Its differential, evaluated on T₀,…,Tⱼ ∈ p_(ℂ) , is (dω)(T₀,…,Tⱼ) = ∑_(i = 0)^(j)( − 1)ⁱTᵢ ⋅ ω(T₀,…,T̂ᵢ,…,Tⱼ). The hat denotes omission of an argument. Denote the cohomology of this complex by H^(j)(g,K;V ⊗ Eₘ) . Denote by κⱼ the comparison map induced by their associated homogeneous-frame differential forms: κⱼ : H^(j)(g,K;A_(cusp) ⊗ Eₘ) ⟶ H^(j)(X,ℰₘ). Definition CP-D3-CUSP. Cuspidal Cohomology Define the cuspidal subspace of ordinary cohomology by H_(cusp)^(j)(Γ ,Eₘ) : = im (κⱼ).

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Spectral Notation
text: Spectral Notation Let L_(disc)²(Γ \ G) be the closed Hilbert sum of irreducible subrepresentations of the right regular representation on L²(Γ \ G) . Let L_(cusp)² be the closure of A_(cusp) in L² , and put Lᵣₑₛ² = L_(disc)² ∩ (L_(cusp)²)^(⟂). For a unitary representation V , write V_(K)^(∞) for its smooth vectors that are K -finite. For an irreducible π , abbreviate π_(K) = π_(K)^(∞) . For π in the discrete spectrum, M_(Γ)(π) = Hom_(G) (π,L_(disc)²) is its multiplicity space, where Hom_(G) denotes bounded complex-linear intertwining maps. Discussion The comparison map κⱼ is injective under the arithmetic hypotheses used here, by the external theorem cited in AC7. Defining its image does not prove that injection. Likewise, interior and cuspidal cohomology are different definitions; their equality in this particular degree is the content of CP5.

heading: The Correspondence
text: The Correspondence Theorem CP5. The Degree-Two Cuspidal and Parabolic Correspondence [6, Thm. 7.1]; [11, Thm. 4.3]; [3, Prop. 4.4(i), Prop. 5.4]; [9, App. A, pp. 29–30] Let G/ℚ be a simply connected semisimple group with G(ℝ) ≃ Sp(1,1) and ℚ -rank one, and let Γ be a torsion-free congruence lattice in G . Put X = Γ \ ℋ . For every integer n ≥ 2 , take the complex algebraic coefficient representation Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ , m = n − 2 , with its flat bundle and the transported positive homogeneous metric h^(ℋ) of CP-H1. Then the explicit period construction gives a complex-linear isomorphism , Sₙ^(−)(Γ ) ⊕︎ Sₙ⁺(Γ ) → [∼ []] Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ), , (11) (f_(−),f₊) ⟼ [Ω_(f_(−)) + Ω_(f₊)⁺]. Inside ordinary complex cohomology, Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ) = H_(!)²(X,ℰₘ) = H_(cusp)²(Γ ,Eₘ). With the spectral notation above, , H²(g,K;(Lᵣₑₛ²(Γ \ G))_(K)^(∞) ⊗ Eₘ) = 0., (11a) The restriction map in (6) induces an injection , H²(Γ ,Eₘ)/H_(cusp)²(Γ ,Eₘ) ↪ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),Eₘ)., (11c) Discussion This supplies the analogue of the global Eichler–Shimura step in the present setting. At n = 2 it identifies parabolic cohomology with self-dual and anti-self-dual square-integrable harmonic two-forms with trivial coefficients. The n = 1 Hardy limit is outside (11): there is no coefficient system Sym^(− 1) ℂ⁴ in this construction.

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Eisenstein Classes and the Scope of the Equality
text: Eisenstein Classes and the Scope of the Equality Discussion Vanishing of boundary restriction is a cohomological condition. It does not, by itself, make an automorphic representative cuspidal. In general, interior cohomology can contain residual Eisenstein contributions. Grobner §6.3 explicitly warns about this distinction; a general theorem requiring regular highest weight cannot be applied to our family mμ₁ , whose highest weights lie on a wall. CP5 supplies the additional argument needed here: only tempered discrete series have degree-two unitary cohomology, and Wallach excludes them from the residual spectrum. Grobner §1.2 gives the automorphic decomposition H² = H_(cusp)² ⊕︎ H_(Eis)² , where the second summand is Eisenstein cohomology. His Theorem 6.1 allows nonzero non-square-integrable Eisenstein classes in ordinary H² . Applying the injection (11c) to this complementary summand shows that its boundary restriction is injective. This does not assert that the summand vanishes. The use of all cusp stabilizers, finite-volume arithmetic quotients, complex algebraic coefficients, and degree two is explicit in CP5. Neatness is unnecessary: the finite cusp holonomy is handled by the translation cover and transfer in CP3. The integrability bound n ≥ 5 belongs to the dimension formula below, not to this cohomological correspondence.

text: An Explicit Dimension Formula Discussion The multiplicity formula used below is [6, Prop. 7.1]. Its derivation in §7.2 draws on Arakawa's work on [1] and [2]. Corollary CP6 translates the discrete-series multiplicities into dimensions of regular cusp spinors and parabolic cohomology using CP4 and CP5. Corollary CP6. Dimensions at Principal Congruence Level [6, Prop. 7.1, §7.2]; [1, Thm. 2]; [2, Prop. 5.4] Let D/ℚ be a definite quaternion algebra with discriminant d(D) , and fix a maximal order O . Define the ball realization G_(B) by G_(B)(ℚ) = {g ∈ GL₂ (D) : g^(∗)diag (1, − 1)g = diag (1, − 1)}, where g^(∗) is the quaternionic conjugate transpose. Fix D⊗_(ℚ)ℝ ≃ ℍ , and identify the half-space real group by g ↦ CgC^(− 1) , transporting the rational structure. For an integer N ≥ 3 , let Γ (N) = C{g = (gᵢⱼ) ∈ G_(B)(ℚ) : gᵢⱼ − δᵢⱼ ∈ NO}C^(− 1), N ≥ 3. Write h = h(Γ (N)) for its number of cusps. For every integer n ≥ 5 , , dim_(ℂ) Sₙ^(−)(Γ (N)) = dim_(ℂ) Sₙ⁺(Γ (N)) = h[(N³(n³ − n))/(1440)∏_(p|d(D))(p² + 1) − 1]., (12) For the same N and n , dim_(ℂ) Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ (N),E_(n − 2)) = 2h[(N³(n³ − n))/(1440)∏_(p|d(D))(p² + 1) − 1].

title: Classical Cuspidal and Parabolic Cohomology
heading: Coefficient Fields
text: Coefficient Fields Discussion The cohomological correspondence also gives an arithmetic constraint on Hecke eigenvalues. Its arithmetic input is a coefficient representation over a number field. This must be distinguished from the complex representation used to write the differential forms. The descent statement below uses [8, §20, especially 20.7]; the Hecke correspondence is the restriction–conjugation–transfer construction described in [10, §4.1]. Proposition CP7. A Number-Field Model for Parabolic Cohomology [8, 20.7–20.9] Let G/ℚ be a simply connected semisimple group of rational rank one with G(ℝ) ≃ Sp(1,1) , and let Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) be a torsion-free congruence lattice. Let n ≥ 2 and m = n − 2 . There exist a number field L ⊂ ℂ , an algebraic representation ρ_(m,L) : G_(L) → GL (E_(m,L)) , and an isomorphism , (E_(m,L),ρ_(m,L))⊗_(L)ℂ ≃ (Eₘ,Rₘ), Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴., (13) For every such choice define , H_(L) = ker (H²(Γ ,E_(m,L)) ⟶ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),E_(m,L)))., (14) Then H_(L) is finite-dimensional over L , and scalar extension induces an isomorphism , H_(L)⊗_(L)ℂ ≃ Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Eₘ)., (15) For m = 0 one may take L = ℚ . If m is odd, the complex representation Eₘ of G has no real model, and consequently (13) has no model over ℚ .

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Overview
text: Expository How restriction to cusp groups detects the image of compactly supported cohomology on a hyperbolic four-manifold. Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support A closed differential form on a noncompact manifold can carry cohomology out along its ends. For a finite-volume hyperbolic manifold, each end is a cusp, with a compact cross-section on which one can restrict the class. The classes whose restrictions vanish are precisely those that admit compactly supported closed representatives. Group cohomology describes the same condition by restriction to the cusp subgroups; its kernel is called parabolic cohomology. This gives a useful target for period constructions. If a closed two-form with flat coefficients produces a group two-cocycle, one can test its parabolicity by finding a one-cochain primitive on each cusp group. The theorem below explains why this test detects compact support at the level of cohomology. Its proof also describes how to remove a form's tails in the cusps.

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Definition 1 · Interior Cohomology
text: M000001 Definition 1. Interior Cohomology Let ℰ be a finite-dimensional complex flat bundle on a smooth manifold X . The interior cohomology is the image of the forget-support map j_(c) : H_(!)^(q)(X,ℰ) = im (j_(c)) ⊆ H^(q)(X,ℰ).

The degree-two parabolic cohomology is Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,E) = ker (H²(Γ ,E) → [res []] ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),E)). For an empty set of cusps the target is zero.

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Theorem 3 · Concise Proof
text: M000003 Let Y = ∂X̄ . A cusp cross-section lifts to the equivariant inclusion S_(ξ) ↪ ℍ⁴ , so the comparisons from group cohomology to cohomology with local coefficients carry subgroup restriction to restriction on Y . Here the contractible covers give free resolutions ([2, Thm. I.7.5, §III.1]), and the Čech double-complex argument gives the de Rham comparison with flat coefficients ([1, Thms. 8.9, 15.8]). The expanded comparison explains the coefficient extension and naturality. The relative de Rham complex consists of forms on X̄ whose pullbacks to Y vanish. Extension by zero includes the compactly supported forms on X in this complex. On a collar, integration in the normal direction gives a homotopy from the identity to pullback from Y . Applied to a closed relative form, it gives a primitive on the collar that vanishes at Y . Subtracting the differential of a cutoff times this primitive makes the form vanish near Y , without changing its relative class. The same adjustment to a relative primitive proves injectivity. Thus extension by zero identifies H_(c)²(X,ℰ) with H²(X̄,Y;ℰ) , compatibly with their maps to ordinary cohomology. Every form on Y extends to X̄ by parallel transport along a collar followed by a cutoff. Restriction is therefore surjective in each degree. Its kernel is the relative complex, so the associated long exact sequence, under the comparisons just described, is (3). Exactness identifies the kernel of cusp restriction with im (j_(c)) and the kernel of j_(c) with im (∂) . This proves (2) and (4). The resulting condition has concrete representatives on both sides. A group cocycle restricts to zero in cohomology exactly when it has a one-cochain primitive as in (1). For a closed form with exact restriction to every cusp cross-section, the interval homotopy extends a primitive along each cusp. Subtracting its differential after multiplication by a cutoff equal to one sufficiently far out removes the tails. The resulting closed form has compact support and represents the original ordinary class.

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Theorem 3 · Expanded Proof
text: M000003 We first identify the restriction map in the relative cohomology sequence with cusp-group restriction. Keep the notation ℰ for the extended local system on X̄ , and push the boundary a short distance into X along the collars. The resulting inclusion of a cusp cross-section lifts to the Γ_(ξ) -equivariant inclusion S_(ξ) ↪ ℍ⁴ . Since both covering spaces are contractible, it induces the inclusion Γ_(ξ) ⊂ Γ on fundamental groups, with the chosen lifts fixing the coefficient identifications. First compare group cohomology with singular cohomology. If Z is X or a cross-section, and G is its deck group, the augmented singular chain complex C_(∗)(Z̃;ℂ) is a free resolution of the trivial ℂ[G] -module: the action on lifted simplices is free, and the augmented complex is exact because Z̃ is contractible. Thus Hom_(ℂ[G]) (C_(∗)(Z̃;ℂ),E) computes H^(∗)(G,E) by the comparison theorem for projective resolutions ([2, Thm. I.7.5, p. 24]). It is also the singular cochain complex with local coefficients: a cochain assigns a vector to each lifted simplex, equivariantly under the deck group. We use the differential δu = u ∘ ∂ ; Brown's signed Hom-complex convention has the same cocycles and coboundaries (§III.1, pp.57–59). For a subgroup H ⊂ G , a free ℂ[G] -resolution remains free after restriction to H . The map on lifted chains therefore computes subgroup restriction, by the uniqueness up to chain homotopy in the same comparison theorem. This is the functoriality described in [2, §III.8, pp. 78–80]. To pass from singular cohomology to differential forms, we use a common Čech complex. Choose a locally finite good cover U of Z : every nonempty finite intersection is contractible. Let ℒ denote the local system of parallel sections of ℰ . The Čech cochain space C [ˇ]^(p)(U,ℒ) = ∏_(i₀ < ⋯ < iₚ)ℒ(U_(i₀) ∩ ⋯ ∩ U_(iₚ)) has differential given by alternating restriction. For differential forms, consider the double complex ∏_(i₀ < ⋯ < iₚ)Ω^(q)(U_(i₀) ∩ ⋯ ∩ U_(iₚ),ℰ) , with total differential δ [ˇ] + ( − 1)^(p)d_(∇) . Its augmented rows are exact by the partition-of-unity homotopy. Its columns have cohomology only in degree zero, where they are parallel sections: each intersection has a parallel frame and the Poincaré lemma applies componentwise. Computing total cohomology in the two orders identifies de Rham cohomology with H^(∗)(C [ˇ]^(∗)(U,ℒ)) . For singular cochains with local coefficients, form the analogous Čech double complex. Use chains whose simplices lie in a member of the cover. Subdivision and its prism homotopy identify their cohomology with ordinary singular cohomology. The augmented Čech rows are exact: for each such simplex, the nonempty set of cover members containing it gives a contractible augmented simplicial complex. On an intersection, the coefficient system is constant and contractibility gives cohomology only in degree zero, again equal to its parallel sections. Thus the same Čech complex computes singular cohomology. These are the double-complex arguments of [1, Prop. 8.8, Thm. 8.9, Prop. 15.2, Thm. 15.8]. Their stated comparison theorems use constant coefficients; the argument above explains the extension to the flat bundle used here. On overlaps, changes of parallel frame are locally constant and commute with differentiation and coefficient transport. No global trivialization is required. Restriction and refinement give maps of these augmented complexes. For the cross-section inclusion, refine its cover by the inverse images of a cover of X ; the resulting pullback maps commute with both augmentations. A common refinement compares any two choices. Hence the comparison respects pullback to each cusp cross-section. Finally, pushing the boundary into a collar identifies the ordinary cohomology of X̄ with that of its interior and identifies boundary restriction with restriction to that cross-section. This gives the absolute and boundary comparisons in (3). It remains to identify the relative term with compactly supported cohomology. Let i : ∂X̄ ↪ X̄ denote boundary inclusion. Define , Ω^(q)(X̄,∂X̄;ℰ) = {ω ∈ Ω^(q)(X̄,ℰ) : i^(∗)ω = 0}., (5) We use the cohomology of (5) as the relative de Rham group H^(q)(X̄,∂X̄;ℰ) . A compactly supported form on X extends smoothly by zero near the boundary, giving a map into this complex. We prove that this map induces an isomorphism in degree two. Choose a collar Y × [0,ε) , where Y = ∂X̄ , with boundary coordinate s = 0 . Parallel transport identifies the bundle there with the pullback of ℰ|_(Y) . In this identification write a form as ω = α(s) + ds ∧ β(s), (Kω)(s) = ∫₀^(s)β(u) du. The operator K lowers degree by one. If p : Y × [0,ε) → Y is projection, differentiation and the fundamental theorem of calculus give , d_(∇)Kω + Kd_(∇)ω = ω − p^(∗)i^(∗)ω., (6) The integral uses parallel transport along the interval, so it is defined for a flat bundle with arbitrary monodromy on Y . For a closed relative two-form ω , (6) says ω = d_(∇)Kω on the collar. Choose a smooth scalar function χ equal to one near s = 0 and supported in the collar. Extend χKω by zero outside the collar. Its boundary pullback is zero because Kω is zero at s = 0 . Therefore , ω₀ = ω − d_(∇)(χKω), (7) is in the same relative class and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary. Since X̄ is compact, ω₀|_(X) has compact support. This proves surjectivity. For injectivity, suppose a compactly supported closed two-form ω₀ is d_(∇)η for a relative one-form η on X̄ . On a sufficiently small collar, ω₀ = 0 , so d_(∇)η = 0 there. Since i^(∗)η = 0 , (6) gives η = d_(∇)Kη on that collar. With χ supported there, replace η by η₀ = η − d_(∇)(χKη). Then η₀ vanishes near the boundary and d_(∇)η₀ = ω₀ . It is the required compactly supported primitive. Both directions used the inclusion of the compact-support complex, so the comparison takes the relative-to-absolute map to j_(c) . We can now apply the relative cohomology sequence. Extending a form on Y by parallel transport along the collar, and multiplying by a cutoff equal to one at Y , proves degreewise surjectivity of i^(∗) . Hence there is a short exact sequence of complexes , 0 ⟶ Ω^(∗)(X̄,Y;ℰ) ⟶ Ω^(∗)(X̄,ℰ) → [i^(∗) []] Ω^(∗)(Y,ℰ) ⟶ 0., (8) Its long exact sequence contains H¹(X̄,ℰ) ⟶ H¹(Y,ℰ) → [∂ []] H²(X̄,Y;ℰ) ⟶ H²(X̄,ℰ) ⟶ H²(Y,ℰ). The group and de Rham comparisons identify the absolute and boundary terms, while extension by zero identifies the relative term with H_(c)²(X,ℰ) . The resulting sequence is (3). In particular, its last map has kernel Φ₂(Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,E)) , whereas exactness identifies that kernel with im (j_(c)) . The connecting map has an explicit description. Represent a class of H¹(Y,ℰ) by a closed form θ and extend it to θ̃ on X̄ . Then d_(∇)θ̃ is relative, and , ∂[θ] = [d_(∇)θ̃]ᵣₑₗ., (9) A different extension changes this by the differential of a relative form. A change of θ by an exact boundary form also leaves the relative class unchanged. Thus (9) is well-defined. Its absolute class is zero, and exactness says that every element of ker (j_(c)) arises this way. Exactness at H¹(Y,ℰ) further says that a boundary class contributes zero under ∂ exactly when it extends as a cohomology class over X̄ . Finally, we describe the condition in terms of cocycles and forms. For a group cocycle, the restriction of [c] is zero precisely when c|_(Γ_(ξ)²) = δb_(ξ) for some one-cochain, which is (1). For the form construction, let α be any closed two-form representing a class with zero cusp restrictions. Write a cusp end as Y_(ξ) × [0,∞) , with height t increasing toward infinity, and let i₀ be inclusion at t = 0 . Vanishing of the restriction gives a one-form θ_(ξ) on Y_(ξ) such that i₀^(∗)α = d_(∇)θ_(ξ). Use the same interval homotopy as in (6), now integrating from 0 to t . On the end it gives β_(ξ) = p^(∗)θ_(ξ) + Kα, d_(∇)β_(ξ) = α. Choose a smooth χ_(ξ)(t) equal to zero near t = 0 and equal to one for all sufficiently large t . Extend χ_(ξ)β_(ξ) by zero across the base of the end. There are finitely many ends, so the form , α_(c) = α − d_(∇)(∑_([ξ])χ_(ξ)β_(ξ)), (10) is smooth, closed, compactly supported, and cohomologous to α . Every integral in this construction has a finite interval of integration. Thus the construction requires no decay estimate at infinity. It realizes the lift supplied by the relative exact sequence. Different choices can give different compact-support classes, but (4) identifies their difference as an element of im (∂) .

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: The Geometry of the Ends
text: The Geometry of the Ends Let ℍ⁴ be real hyperbolic four-space, and let Γ ⊂ Isom (ℍ⁴) be a discrete torsion-free group such that X = Γ \ ℍ⁴ is of finite volume. The metric on X is complete. Choose one parabolic fixed point ξ at infinity for each cusp, and write Γ_(ξ) = {γ ∈ Γ : γξ = ξ} for its full stabilizer. The cusp decomposition gives finitely many ends with cross-sections Y_(ξ) = Γ_(ξ) \ S_(ξ) , where S_(ξ) is a horosphere isometric to Euclidean three-space. Each Y_(ξ) is compact and flat. Truncation gives a compact core; reparametrizing its attached cusp collars gives a compact manifold X̄ with interior X and boundary ∂X̄ = ∐_([ξ])Y_(ξ). The compactification has the same homotopy type as X . The geometric input is the finite-volume cusp theorem: [3, §4.2.5, Prop. 4.2.17, Cor. 4.2.18]. When X is compact, take X̄ = X and an empty boundary. Fix a finite-dimensional complex vector space E and a representation ρ : Γ → GL (E) . It defines the flat bundle ℰ = Γ \ (ℍ⁴ × E), γ ⋅ (z,v) = (γz,ρ(γ)v). A lifted section is therefore an E -valued function satisfying f(γz) = ρ(γ)f(z) . In a local parallel frame, the flat differential d_(∇) is the ordinary differential applied to each component. The same local system extends over X̄ : on a cusp product, parallel transport along the interval identifies it with the pullback of its restriction to Y_(ξ) .

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: The Two Cohomological Conditions
text: The Two Cohomological Conditions Let ℰ be a finite-dimensional complex flat bundle on a smooth manifold X , with flat differential d_(∇) . Write Ω^(q)(X,ℰ) for its smooth differential q -forms and Ω_(c)^(q)(X,ℰ) for the forms with compact support. Set both spaces to zero in negative degree. Define H^(q)(X,ℰ) = (ker (d_(∇) : Ω^(q) → Ω^(q + 1)))/(d_(∇)Ω^(q − 1)), H_(c)^(q)(X,ℰ) = (ker (d_(∇) : Ω_(c)^(q) → Ω_(c)^(q + 1)))/(d_(∇)Ω_(c)^(q − 1)). The inclusion of complexes induces the forget-support map j_(c) : H_(c)^(q)(X,ℰ) ⟶ H^(q)(X,ℰ). Definition 1. Interior Cohomology Let ℰ be a finite-dimensional complex flat bundle on a smooth manifold X . The interior cohomology is the image of the forget-support map j_(c) : H_(!)^(q)(X,ℰ) = im (j_(c)) ⊆ H^(q)(X,ℰ). Thus H_(!)² consists of ordinary classes with a compactly supported closed representative. The map j_(c) can lose information: a compactly supported form may have an ordinary primitive but no compactly supported primitive. The exact sequence in the theorem will identify this kernel. For group cohomology we use left coefficients, so γ acts on E as ρ(γ) . An inhomogeneous one-cochain is any function b : Γ → E , and a two-cochain is any function c : Γ² → E . Their differentials in the relevant degrees are (δb)(g,h) = ρ(g)b(h) − b(gh) + b(g), (δc)(g,h,k) = ρ(g)c(h,k) − c(gh,k) + c(g,hk) − c(g,h). The equation δc = 0 defines two-cocycles, and H²(Γ ,E) is their quotient by the two-coboundaries δb . Restriction of functions defines the maps for subgroups. Definition 2. Parabolic Cohomology Let Γ ⊂ Isom (ℍ⁴) be discrete and torsion-free with finite-volume quotient, let E be a finite-dimensional complex left Γ -module, and let Γ_(ξ) be the full stabilizer of a chosen point representing each cusp. The degree-two parabolic cohomology is Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,E) = ker (H²(Γ ,E) → [res []] ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),E)). For an empty set of cusps the target is zero. For a two-cocycle c , the condition in this definition is the existence, for every cusp, of a single function b_(ξ) : Γ_(ξ) → E satisfying , c(u,v) = ρ(u)b_(ξ)(v) − b_(ξ)(uv) + b_(ξ)(u) (u,v ∈ Γ_(ξ))., (1) The same b_(ξ) must work for all pairs in that cusp group. Replacing c by c + δa replaces a possible primitive by b_(ξ) + a|_(Γ_(ξ)) , so this is a condition on the cohomology class.

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Parabolic Cohomology Is Interior Cohomology
text: Parabolic Cohomology Is Interior Cohomology The contractible universal cover of X identifies group cohomology with cohomology of the flat bundle. Denote this comparison by Φ_(q) : H^(q)(Γ ,E) → [∼ []] H^(q)(X,ℰ). Likewise, the universal cover S_(ξ) ≃ ℝ³ identifies H^(q)(Γ_(ξ),E) with H^(q)(Y_(ξ),ℰ|_(Y_(ξ))) . These comparisons carry subgroup restriction to restriction on the cusp cross-sections, as we verify in the proof. Theorem 3. The Cusp Restriction Exact Sequence [1, §§8, 15]; [2, Thm. I.7.5, §§III.1, III.8]; [3, Prop. 4.2.17, Cor. 4.2.18] Let Γ ⊂ Isom (ℍ⁴) be a discrete torsion-free group with finite-volume quotient X , and let E be a finite-dimensional complex representation of Γ , with associated flat bundle ℰ . Use the full cusp stabilizers Γ_(ξ) . Under the comparison Φ₂ : H²(Γ ,E) ≃ H²(X,ℰ) , , Φ₂(Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,E)) = H_(!)²(X,ℰ)., (2) More precisely, the relative cohomology sequence of a cusp compactification gives the exact sequence , H¹(X,ℰ) → [res []] ⨁_([ξ])H¹(Γ_(ξ),E) → [∂ []] H_(c)²(X,ℰ) → [j_(c) []] H²(X,ℰ) → [res []] ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),E)., (3) Here res is subgroup restriction transported by the comparisons, and ∂ is the relative connecting homomorphism transported to compactly supported cohomology. In particular, , ker (j_(c)), = im (∂),; H_(!)²(X,ℰ), ≃ H_(c)²(X,ℰ)/ im (∂)., (4)

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: Why the Whole Cusp Group Matters
text: Why the Whole Cusp Group Matters Example. A Two-Cocycle on a Torus Cusp For a cusp group ℤ³ with trivial coefficients ℂ , use additive notation and set c(u,v) = u₁v₂. Bilinearity gives δc = 0 . A two-coboundary for this trivial action has the form b(v) − b(u + v) + b(u) and is symmetric in u,v . Our cocycle is not symmetric: c(e₁,e₂) = 1 while c(e₂,e₁) = 0 . Consequently its class on ℤ³ is nonzero. Nevertheless it becomes a coboundary on every cyclic subgroup. For a nonzero a ∈ ℤ³ , define on the subgroup generated by a b(ka) = − (k(k − 1))/(2)a₁a₂ (k ∈ ℤ). Then (δb)(ka,ℓa) = kℓa₁a₂ = c(ka,ℓa) . The zero subgroup causes no difficulty. Thus cyclic tests do not detect the two-dimensional obstruction on a cusp cross-section.

title: Parabolic Cohomology and Compact Support
heading: The Role in Automorphic Cohomology
text: The Role in Automorphic Cohomology Suppose an automorphic construction supplies a closed two-form α with flat coefficients and a period two-cocycle c satisfying Φ₂([c]) = [α] . If α restricts to an exact form on every cusp cross-section, the cutoff formula (10) gives a compactly supported representative of [α] , and [c] lies in parabolic cohomology. Equivalently, one can check this boundary condition by finding a one-cochain primitive for c on each full cusp group, as in equation (1).

title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues
heading: Overview
text: Research Positive quaternionic similitudes, three normalizations, and an integral cohomology lattice. Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues Discussion The Hecke-equivariant period map extends from isometries to positive similitudes. There are several natural extensions of the central action. The extension compatible with the untwisted coefficient representation gives algebraicity; a different extension preserves integral coefficients on the integral Hecke semigroup and gives algebraic integers. SH1 specifies the normalizations, SH2 extends the cohomological comparison, and SH3 proves integrality. The central example in SH4 shows why integrality cannot be asserted independently of normalization and the chosen semigroup. The proofs apply to either spinor chirality, for weights n ≥ 2 .

title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues

heading: Theorem SH2 · Similitude equivariance and algebraic eigenvalues
text: SH2 Theorem SH2. Similitude equivariance and algebraic eigenvalues For the data of SH-D2, (7) defines endomorphisms of Sₙ^(±)(Γ ) . The C- and I-operators in (8) are L -linear endomorphisms of H_(L) = Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,E_(m,L)). For either chirality, the injective period map intertwines the corresponding operators. Every eigenvalue of a C-, I-, or U-operator on a nonzero cusp spinor is algebraic over ℚ . For any commuting family indexed by A ⊂ G̃⁺(ℚ) and any nonzero simultaneous eigenform, the fields generated over L by its C- and I-eigenvalues are equal and finite over L . If these eigenvalues are denoted by λ_(α)^(C) and λ_(α)^(I) and the U-eigenvalue by λ_(α)^(U) , then , λ_(α)^(I) = ν(α)^(m)λ_(α)^(C) = ν(α)^(m/2)λ_(α)^(U)., (9) For even n , the U-eigenvalues generate that same field over L . Conjugation by a rational similitude is a rational automorphism of the isometry group. Clearing denominators shows that it commensurates Γ . Thus p₁,p₂ are finite coverings. The coefficient maps in (8) intertwine the two Γ_(α) actions, since α^(†) = ν(α)α^(− 1) . They are defined over L . Properness of both coverings and trace compatibility with compact support prove preservation of interior, hence parabolic, cohomology as in CP8. Every αᵢ has multiplier ν(α) , and every slash summand is a constant scalar multiple of f|ₙg_(αᵢ) . The latter is regular by SH1. Its lift is g ↦ F_(f)(g_(αᵢ)g) , so right central finiteness and moderate growth persist. With Δᵢ = Γ ∩ αᵢ^(− 1)Γ αᵢ , change of variables gives ∫_(Δᵢ \ G)‖F_(f)(g_(αᵢ)g)‖ₙ² dg = [Γ : αᵢΔᵢαᵢ^(− 1)]∫_(Γ \ G)‖F_(f)(g)‖ₙ² dg. It is finite by CP1. Taking a common finite cover for the finitely many summands and using the triangle inequality proves finite norm for their sum. The right-action and coset identities prove Γ -automorphy and independence of representatives. CP1 then proves cuspidality. The trace calculation of CP8 applies unchanged, and (6) identifies it term by term with the spinor sum. Reflection gives the same calculation for the plus space: ν(θ(α)) = ν(α) and θ intertwines the coefficient transports through Rₘ(W) . The period map is injective by AC7 and reflection. The characteristic-polynomial and finite-dimensional Hecke-algebra arguments of CP9 therefore prove algebraicity and the finite-field assertion for C and I. Their fields are equal because their eigenvalues differ by nonzero rational factors ν(α)^(m) . Equation (5) proves (9); its multiplier is algebraic, giving individual algebraicity for U as well. title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues
heading: Theorem SH3 · Algebraic integers for integral similitudes
text: SH3 Theorem SH3. Algebraic integers for integral similitudes Fix a maximal order O ⊂ D , and put , G(O) = {γ ∈ M₂(O) : γ^(∗)Hγ = H}, Δ_(O)⁺ = M₂(O) ∩ G̃⁺(ℚ)., (10) Let Γ ⊆ G(O) be a torsion-free congruence subgroup. Let O_(L) be the ring of integers of L . There exists a finitely generated O_(L) -submodule M ⊂ H_(L) with M⊗_(O_(L))L = H_(L) such that , T_(α)^(I)M ⊆ M (α ∈ Δ_(O)⁺)., (11) For every α ∈ Δ_(O)⁺ , every eigenvalue of T_(α)^(I , ±) on a nonzero regular cusp spinor is an algebraic integer. Equivalently, for α ∈ Δ_(O)⁺ the numbers ν(α)^(m)λ_(α)^(C) and ν(α)^(m/2)λ_(α)^(U) are algebraic integers. For a simultaneous eigenform of a commuting family in Δ_(O)⁺ , all these eigenvalues lie in the ring of integers of one number field. Construct the coefficient lattice. Choose a full O_(L) -lattice Λ₀ ⊂ W_(L) and a ℤ -basis a₁,…,a₁₆ of M₂(O) . Put Λ = ∑_(j = 1)¹⁶R_(L)(aⱼ)Λ₀. It is finitely generated, torsion-free, and spans W_(L) . It contains Λ₀ because the order contains the identity. Products of basis elements are integral linear combinations of the basis, so the order preserves Λ . Let Λₘ ⊂ E_(m,L) be the image of Sym_(O_(L))^(m) Λ . It is a full lattice and is preserved by the symmetric power of every element of the order. No division by m ! is used. To see that reduced traces and norms are integral, let x ∈ O act by left multiplication on the finite free abelian group O . Its integer characteristic polynomial annihilates x , so x is integral over ℤ . If x is noncentral, its degree-two minimal polynomial is its reduced characteristic polynomial; its coefficients are rational algebraic integers, hence integers. If x is central, it is a rational algebraic integer, and the same conclusion follows directly. Consequently quaternionic conjugation preserves the order: for x ∈ O , x̄ = trd (x) − x and the reduced trace is integral. Hence α^(†) = Hα^(∗)H belongs to M₂(O) whenever α does. For γ ∈ G(O) , both γ and γ^(− 1) = γ^(†) preserve Λ , so Λₘ defines an integral local system on X . The Hecke coefficient map is integral. If α ∈ Δ_(O)⁺ , its multiplier is a positive integer: the first diagonal entry of α^(∗)Hα is the difference of two integral reduced norms and equals ν(α) . Every representative in Γ αΓ lies in M₂(O) . Thus ν(α)^(m)ρ̃_(m,L)(α)^(− 1) = ρ̃_(m,L)(α^(†)) preserves Λₘ . This gives a morphism of integral local systems from p₂^(∗)Λₘ to p₁^(∗)Λₘ . It need not be an isomorphism over O_(L) . Pullback and trace are also integral; trace sums over sheets and does not divide by their number. Pass to integral parabolic cohomology. Define Hₚₐᵣ²(Γ ,Λₘ) = ker (H²(Γ ,Λₘ) ⟶ ⨁_([ξ])H²(Γ_(ξ),Λₘ)) and let M be its image in H_(L) . The compact-core relative cohomology sequence identifies this kernel with the image of compactly supported cohomology, over O_(L) as well as over L . Proper pullback, the integral coefficient morphism, and trace preserve that image. Therefore they preserve M . The finite cellular complexes for the compact core and its boundary show that M is finitely generated. Localization to L is exact, so it commutes with cohomology and with the kernel of restriction. It follows that M ⊗ L = H_(L) . As a subgroup of an L -vector space, M is torsion-free; its underlying abelian group is therefore a finite-rank free ℤ -module. Each operator in (11) is represented on it by an integer matrix and satisfies a monic polynomial in ℤ[t] . The same polynomial annihilates its action on H_(L)⊗_(L)ℂ . By the injective Hecke comparison, every cusp-spinor eigenvalue is a root and is an algebraic integer. Finally SH2 supplies one finite number field for a simultaneous system; its integral elements form that field's ring of integers.

title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues
heading: Why the normalization and semigroup matter
text: Why the normalization and semigroup matter Proposition SH4. Central scalars and the minimal coefficient twist For t ∈ ℚ_(> 0) , the central double coset Γ (tI)Γ has one left coset, and on either cusp-spinor space , T_(tI)^(U) = 1, T_(tI)^(C) = t^(− m), T_(tI)^(I) = t^(m)., (12) If m > 0 and the cusp-spinor space is nonzero, T_(pI)^(C) has the nonintegral eigenvalue p^(− m) for every rational prime p , while T_(p^(− 1)I)^(I) has the same nonintegral eigenvalue. For the standard symplectic form J₄ = (0, I₂; − I₂, 0) over ℚₚ , put Aₚ = diag (p,p,1,1) , so its multiplier is p . For an integer e , the map p^(e)Sym^(m) (Aₚ^(− 1)) preserves Sym^(m) ℤₚ⁴ if and only if e ≥ m . Discussion The last assertion shows that ν^(m) is the smallest uniform integral power correcting the inverse coefficient transport on this standard local lattice. Combined with the degree-two factor ν² in SH1, it explains the exponent n = m + 2 in the integral spinor slash action. It is a statement about coefficient lattices; it does not exclude extra divisibility after taking a particular Hecke trace or passing to a particular cohomology group. The central example also separates two different assertions. Integral positive similitudes give algebraic integers in the I-normalization. The full rational similitude group contains inverses of integral central scalars, so it does not have the same blanket integrality property. No division by the double-coset degree is part of SH3.

title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues
heading: Published conventions and further comparisons
text: Published conventions and further comparisons Discussion [1, §2, §§5.1–5.3] define adelic similitude forms with trivial central character, local Hecke operators, and additional rescalings for their spinor Euler factors. Such an Euler-factor normalization must be distinguished from both a unitary action and an integral coefficient action. The ball-model dictionary is AS3. The formulas above specify rational double-coset correspondences on a fixed arithmetic quotient. Matching them generator by generator with a full adelic Hecke algebra requires tracking the finite adelic components, the chosen quaternionic lattices at ramified primes, the direction of the correspondence, and the central character. A different normalization cannot inherit the integrality label without this comparison. Explicit eigenforms and the arithmetic of their periods remain useful next examples.

title: Similitude Hecke operators and integral eigenvalues
heading: Galois representations
text: Galois representations The Langlands and Galois article explains the four-dimensional spin representation, its five-dimensional standard quotient construction, and the published existence theorem for general-type adelic constituents of weight n ≥ 3 . Its Satake normalization is explicit; identifying it with individual double-coset generators requires the adelic dictionary discussed above.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Overview
text: Expository Four-dimensional spin representations, five-dimensional standard representations, and published transfer theorems for quaternionic cusp forms. Langlands parameters and Galois representations Discussion A Hecke eigenvalue system of regular automorphic spinors has a natural place in the Langlands programme. For the quaternionic similitude group, the spin representation of the dual group has dimension four. For the derived group, the standard representation of the dual group has dimension five. These are related representations of the same arithmetic data, rather than dimensions determined by the spinor fibre Vₙ . There is a published existence theorem for the general-type cuspidal representations in this family when n ≥ 3 : LG3 specifies its hypotheses. It combines transfer from the quaternionic inner form with the Galois representations attached to genus-two Siegel modular forms. The qualifications at n = 2 , for endoscopic forms, and at the Hardy endpoint are explained separately below.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Definition LG-D2 · Weak Equivalence and General Type
text: LG-D2 Definition LG-D2. Weak Equivalence and General Type [4, §§1, 9] Weak equivalence. Two automorphic representations of inner forms are weakly equivalent if their local representations are isomorphic at all but finitely many places where the groups are identified with the split form. CAP. A cuspidal Π of G(A) is CAP if its local representations at almost all places agree with constituents of normalized parabolic induction from an automorphic representation of a Levi subgroup of a proper rational parabolic of H . Weak endoscopy. A cuspidal Π is weakly endoscopic if its unramified parameters at almost all places are the images of automorphic parameters for the proper elliptic endoscopic group GSO(2,2) . General type. A cuspidal Π is of general type if it is neither CAP nor weakly endoscopic.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Proposition LG1 · Dual groups and the exterior-square relation
text: LG1 Proposition LG1. Dual groups and the exterior-square relation The complex dual groups are Ĝ = GSpin₅(ℂ) ≃ GSp₄(ℂ), G^(der) [ˆ] = SO₅(ℂ). Let V be a four-dimensional representation of a group G over a characteristic-zero field, with a nondegenerate alternating form b : V × V ⟶ M valued in a one-dimensional representation M , such that b is G -equivariant. Let c : Λ²V → M be c(v ∧ w) = b(v,w) . Then V₅ = ker (c) ⊗ M^(− 1) is five-dimensional and carries a nondegenerate G -invariant symmetric form with determinant-one action. Moreover, (Λ²V) ⊗ M^(− 1) ≃ 1 ⊕︎ V₅. Replacing (V,M) by (V ⊗ η,M ⊗ η²) for a character η leaves V₅ unchanged. The root datum of the simply connected group of type C₂ is dual to the adjoint root datum of type B₂ , giving SO₅ . Including the similitude centre gives GSpin₅ , whose spin representation identifies it with GSp₄ . Inner twisting leaves these complex dual groups unchanged; their root-data Galois actions are trivial here. The contraction c is onto, so its kernel has dimension 6 − 1 = 5 . In a symplectic basis, the inverse alternating form supplies an equivariant inclusion M ↪ Λ²V whose composite with c is a nonzero scalar. This splits the sequence in characteristic zero. Wedge product gives a symmetric pairing on Λ²V with values in Λ⁴V ≃ M² . The invariant line is nonisotropic; its orthogonal complement is ker (c) . Twisting this complement by M^(− 1) gives the asserted nondegenerate invariant scalar pairing. Finally det (V) = M² , hence det (Λ²V) = M⁶ and det (ker c) = M⁵ ; the twist makes the determinant trivial. The character factors cancel in the last assertion.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Proposition LG2 · From spinor weight to Siegel weight
text: LG2 Proposition LG2. From spinor weight to Siegel weight [6, §§2.1–2.2]; [4, Prop. 8.3] For n ≥ 2 , the infinitesimal character of the discrete series in the adelic hypotheses is the Weyl orbit of (n,1) in the standard C₂ coordinates. Its archimedean Langlands packet on the split group has a holomorphic member of Siegel weight (k₁,k₂) = (n + 1,3), Sym^(n − 2) ⊗ det [3] as a representation of GL₂ . The flat coefficient representation is Eₘ = Sym^(m) ℂ⁴ , of highest weight (m,0) . The half-sum of positive roots of C₂ is (2,1) , so its infinitesimal character is (m + 2,1) = (n,1) . The relative-cohomology calculation CP4 gives this same infinitesimal character for both chiral discrete series; dualizing Eₘ does not change its derived-group highest weight. In the conventions of Weiss §2.1, the discrete-series parameter with infinitesimal character (m₁,m₂) has spin restriction to W_(ℂ) with angular exponents ± (m₁ + m₂) and ± (m₁ − m₂) . Section 2.2 gives holomorphic weight (m₁ + 1,m₂ + 2) . Substitution of (m₁,m₂) = (n,1) gives (n + 1,3) . Since n ≥ 2 , these satisfy k₁ ≥ k₂ ≥ 3 , the cohomological Siegel-weight range.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Theorem LG3 · Spin Galois representations for general-type constituents
text: LG3 Theorem LG3. Spin Galois representations for general-type constituents [4, Props. 8.3, 10.1, Thm. 11.5]; [6, Thm. 3.1, Remark 3.2]; [5]; [3]; [7] Let n ≥ 3 and let Π be a general-type cuspidal automorphic constituent satisfying the adelic hypotheses. There are a number field E ⊂ ℂ , a finite set S of rational primes, and, for every finite place λ of E of residue characteristic ℓ , a continuous semisimple representation r_(Π ,λ) : Gal (ℚ̄/ℚ) ⟶ GSp₄(Ē_(λ)) with the following properties. Here E_(λ) is the completion of E at λ , Ē_(λ) an algebraic closure, and comparisons with complex parameters use compatible embeddings of the algebraic coefficient fields. The representation is unramified at every p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} . Let sₚ be the unitary-normalized unramified Satake conjugacy class of Πₚ at p ∉ S , with convention Lₚ(s,Π ,spin) = det (1 − spin(sₚ)p^(− s))^(− 1) . Define Pₚ(T) = det (1 − p^((n + 1)/2)spin(sₚ)T). Then Pₚ(T) ∈ E[T] is independent of λ , and for p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} , det (1 − r_(Π ,λ)(Frobₚ)T) = Pₚ(T), where Frobₚ denotes arithmetic Frobenius. The representation at ℓ is de Rham, and is crystalline if ℓ ∉ S . With the convention that the cyclotomic character ε_(ℓ) has Hodge–Tate weight 1 , its Hodge–Tate weights are {0,1,n,n + 1}. Its similitude character is χ_(λ)ε_(ℓ)^(n + 1) , where χ_(λ) is the finite-order character attached to the central character of the split transfer, with the reciprocity convention in Weiss Remark 3.2. Each complex conjugate of a Frobenius eigenvalue at p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} has absolute value p^((n + 1)/2) . For ℓ ≥ 5 , r_(Π ,λ) is irreducible. Put m = n − 2 > 0 . The derived coefficient highest weight is (m,0) , whose two coordinates are unequal. Rösner–Weissauer §8 and Proposition 8.3 show that its unitary cohomological archimedean representations are discrete series and contribute only in degree two. Thus it satisfies the inner form's regularity condition used in Theorem 11.5. This condition is specific to the inner form; it is not a claim that (m,0) is strictly dominant for every root of C₂ . To match the algebraic coefficient's central action in that theorem, use the cohomological normalization Π ⊗ |ν|_(A)^(− m/2) , where |ν|_(A) is the product of the local normalized absolute values. At a positive real scalar tI , this twist acts by t^(− m) and cancels the action t^(m) on Eₘ . Apply Theorem 11.5 in that normalization and undo the same twist on the split side. Twisting preserves cuspidality and the general-type condition. This gives a cuspidal generic cohomological representation Π^(′) of GSp₄(A) , with the same unramified factors outside a finite set and the corresponding archimedean packet. By Proposition 10.1 that global packet is a product of local packets. We can therefore replace its archimedean generic member by the holomorphic member without changing the finite factors. Call the resulting cuspidal representation Π^(hol) . Its weight is (n + 1,3) by LG2. Weiss Theorem 3.1 applies because n + 1 ≥ 3 and k₂ = 3 . It supplies the symplectic compatible system, de Rham and crystalline assertions, purity, and irreducibility for ℓ ≥ 5 . It summarizes the constructions of Taylor, Laumon, and Weissauer and subsequent refinements; these are external theorem inputs, not consequences of the ball's de Rham complex. The Hodge–Tate formula in that theorem is {0,k₂ − 2,k₁ − 1,k₁ + k₂ − 3} , which becomes {0,1,n,n + 1} . Its local normalization is Πₚ^(hol) ⊗ |ν|ₚ^(− (n + 1)/2) . Since |p|ₚ = p^(− 1) , this multiplies the spin Satake eigenvalues by p^((n + 1)/2) and gives the displayed polynomial. Remark 3.2 gives the similitude character. Enlarge S to contain the quaternion discriminant, ramified places, and any exceptions in the weak transfer. The shared unramified parameters give all the stated assertions for Π .

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Corollary LG4 · The five-dimensional standard Galois representation
text: LG4 Corollary LG4. The five-dimensional standard Galois representation For r = r_(Π ,λ) in LG3 and μ = sim (r) , the representation r_(5,λ) = ker (Λ²r ⟶ μ) ⊗ μ^(− 1) has image in SO₅(Ē_(λ)) . It is de Rham with Hodge–Tate weights { − n, − 1,0,1,n}, and is unchanged by a character twist of r . LG1 proves the dimension, form, determinant, and twist invariance. Taking exterior powers, kernels of the displayed direct-sum splitting, and tensor products preserves the de Rham property. The pairwise sums of 0,1,n,n + 1 are 1,n,n + 1,n + 1,n + 2,2n + 1 . Subtract the weight n + 1 of μ , then remove the invariant zero-weight line. This gives the five displayed weights.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Proposition LG5 · The Galois representation of a specified endoscopic system
text: LG5 Proposition LG5. The Galois representation of a specified endoscopic system [2, exposé 355]; [1, Thm. 2.2.3, §2.4] Let n ≥ 2 . Let f and g be normalized holomorphic cuspidal eigenforms of weights n + 2 and n , with the same finite-order nebentypus χ . At primes outside their levels write P_(f,p)(T) = 1 − aₚ(f)T + χ(p)p^(n + 1)T², P_(g,p)(T) = 1 − aₚ(g)T + χ(p)p^(n − 1)T². For a compatible coefficient embedding, let r_(f,λ) and r_(g,λ) be their two-dimensional Galois representations, normalized to have these arithmetic Frobenius polynomials. Then r_(λ) = r_(f,λ) ⊕︎ (r_(g,λ) ⊗ ε_(ℓ)) is symplectic with similitude character χ_(λ)ε_(ℓ)^(n + 1) , Hodge–Tate weights {0,1,n,n + 1} , and good-prime polynomial det (1 − r_(λ)(Frobₚ)T) = P_(f,p)(T)P_(g,p)(pT). Every continuous semisimple four-dimensional Galois representation with the same polynomials at all but finitely many primes is isomorphic to r_(λ) . For a two-dimensional representation the exterior-product alternating form has multiplier its determinant. Here the two determinants are both χ_(λ)ε_(ℓ)^(n + 1) , so the orthogonal direct sum of the alternating forms is a nondegenerate alternating form with this multiplier. The Hodge–Tate weights of the classical representation are {0,n + 1} and {0,n − 1} ; tensoring the second by ε_(ℓ) shifts its weights to {1,n} . Arithmetic Frobenius acts on that twist by multiplication by p , proving the polynomial identity. Equality of polynomials gives equality of traces on a dense set by Chebotarev; continuity and the characteristic-zero Brauer–Nesbitt theorem give the final semisimple isomorphism.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Groups and the adelic input
text: Groups and the adelic input Let D/ℚ be a definite quaternion algebra, H = diag (1, − 1) , and let G be the algebraic group G(A) = {g ∈ GL₂ (D⊗_(ℚ)A) : g^(∗)Hg = ν(g)H, ν(g) ∈ A^(×)} for a commutative ℚ -algebra A . After extending scalars to a splitting field of D , this is the symplectic similitude group. Its split inner form is therefore H = GSp₄ , and the identity G^(der) = ker ν descends from the corresponding identity for GSp₄ . Write A = ℝ × A_(f) for the adele ring of ℚ . Write Vₐ = Sym^(a) ℂ² ; the compact group is Sp(1) × Sp(1) . The central character notation means F(zg) = ω(z)F(g) and square integrability is taken modulo the centre. For weight n , set m = n − 2 . For n ≥ 2 , let Π be an irreducible unitary constituent Π ⊂ L_(cusp)²(G(ℚ) \ G(A),ω) with finite-order central character ω , whose archimedean restriction to Sp(1,1) contains the discrete series with minimal compact type V₀ ⊠ Vₙ or Vₙ ⊠ V₀ . We use n as the weight of this constituent. Discussion The similitude group above includes negative real multipliers. Its identity component modulo positive central scalars acts on the ball in the positive-similitude model. The full real group interchanges the two chiralities; a global representation can therefore contain both on restriction. Rösner–Weissauer §8 describes this explicitly. A function on a single quotient Γ \ B must first be placed in the adelic space, with a level and central character, before applying LG3. This is additional data beyond a list of eigenvalues for selected rational double cosets. The theorem is stated for that adelic constituent; it does not infer its existence from algebraicity of a few eigenvalues. Definition LG-D2. Weak Equivalence and General Type [4, §§1, 9] Weak equivalence. Two automorphic representations of inner forms are weakly equivalent if their local representations are isomorphic at all but finitely many places where the groups are identified with the split form. CAP. A cuspidal Π of G(A) is CAP if its local representations at almost all places agree with constituents of normalized parabolic induction from an automorphic representation of a Levi subgroup of a proper rational parabolic of H . Weak endoscopy. A cuspidal Π is weakly endoscopic if its unramified parameters at almost all places are the images of automorphic parameters for the proper elliptic endoscopic group GSO(2,2) . General type. A cuspidal Π is of general type if it is neither CAP nor weakly endoscopic. In the four-dimensional spin representation, the parameters in the weakly endoscopic case are sums of two degree-two parameters with a common determinant. [4, §§1, 9]

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Why four dimensions, and why five also occurs
text: Why four dimensions, and why five also occurs Proposition LG1. Dual groups and the exterior-square relation The complex dual groups are Ĝ = GSpin₅(ℂ) ≃ GSp₄(ℂ), G^(der) [ˆ] = SO₅(ℂ). Let V be a four-dimensional representation of a group G over a characteristic-zero field, with a nondegenerate alternating form b : V × V ⟶ M valued in a one-dimensional representation M , such that b is G -equivariant. Let c : Λ²V → M be c(v ∧ w) = b(v,w) . Then V₅ = ker (c) ⊗ M^(− 1) is five-dimensional and carries a nondegenerate G -invariant symmetric form with determinant-one action. Moreover, (Λ²V) ⊗ M^(− 1) ≃ 1 ⊕︎ V₅. Replacing (V,M) by (V ⊗ η,M ⊗ η²) for a character η leaves V₅ unchanged. Discussion Thus a four-dimensional symplectic Galois representation gives a five-dimensional orthogonal one. The five-dimensional construction forgets central twists. Hecke data for the derived group consequently do not select a unique four-dimensional lift without extra central data.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: The weight dictionary
text: The weight dictionary Proposition LG2. From spinor weight to Siegel weight [6, §§2.1–2.2]; [4, Prop. 8.3] For n ≥ 2 , the infinitesimal character of the discrete series in the adelic hypotheses is the Weyl orbit of (n,1) in the standard C₂ coordinates. Its archimedean Langlands packet on the split group has a holomorphic member of Siegel weight (k₁,k₂) = (n + 1,3), Sym^(n − 2) ⊗ det [3] as a representation of GL₂ .

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: A published existence theorem in this family
text: A published existence theorem in this family Theorem LG3. Spin Galois representations for general-type constituents [4, Props. 8.3, 10.1, Thm. 11.5]; [6, Thm. 3.1, Remark 3.2]; [5]; [3]; [7] Let n ≥ 3 and let Π be a general-type cuspidal automorphic constituent satisfying the adelic hypotheses. There are a number field E ⊂ ℂ , a finite set S of rational primes, and, for every finite place λ of E of residue characteristic ℓ , a continuous semisimple representation r_(Π ,λ) : Gal (ℚ̄/ℚ) ⟶ GSp₄(Ē_(λ)) with the following properties. Here E_(λ) is the completion of E at λ , Ē_(λ) an algebraic closure, and comparisons with complex parameters use compatible embeddings of the algebraic coefficient fields. The representation is unramified at every p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} . Let sₚ be the unitary-normalized unramified Satake conjugacy class of Πₚ at p ∉ S , with convention Lₚ(s,Π ,spin) = det (1 − spin(sₚ)p^(− s))^(− 1) . Define Pₚ(T) = det (1 − p^((n + 1)/2)spin(sₚ)T). Then Pₚ(T) ∈ E[T] is independent of λ , and for p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} , det (1 − r_(Π ,λ)(Frobₚ)T) = Pₚ(T), where Frobₚ denotes arithmetic Frobenius. The representation at ℓ is de Rham, and is crystalline if ℓ ∉ S . With the convention that the cyclotomic character ε_(ℓ) has Hodge–Tate weight 1 , its Hodge–Tate weights are {0,1,n,n + 1}. Its similitude character is χ_(λ)ε_(ℓ)^(n + 1) , where χ_(λ) is the finite-order character attached to the central character of the split transfer, with the reciprocity convention in Weiss Remark 3.2. Each complex conjugate of a Frobenius eigenvalue at p ∉ S ∪ {ℓ} has absolute value p^((n + 1)/2) . For ℓ ≥ 5 , r_(Π ,λ) is irreducible. Discussion The named sources establish this existence direction without appealing to an unspecified complete global Langlands correspondence. The packet and transfer theorems, as well as the Galois construction, are substantial published inputs. Their application here has a supplied argument and awaits independent review; it is not Lean-verified. The normalization in LG3 is intrinsic to the unitary Satake parameter. It must not be identified silently with a chosen double-coset eigenvalue. SH1–SH4 establish integral operators on the ball model; comparison with an adelic Hecke polynomial additionally requires the local generators, their measures, the adelic realization, and its central character. Rational group cohomology gives a field of eigenvalues, as in CP9. A Galois representation is stronger data. In the route above it is obtained from the arithmetic geometry used for Siegel modular forms, after transfer, rather than by giving an unexplained Galois action to H²(Γ ,Eₘ) . Corollary LG4. The five-dimensional standard Galois representation For r = r_(Π ,λ) in LG3 and μ = sim (r) , the representation r_(5,λ) = ker (Λ²r ⟶ μ) ⊗ μ^(− 1) has image in SO₅(Ē_(λ)) . It is de Rham with Hodge–Tate weights { − n, − 1,0,1,n}, and is unchanged by a character twist of r .

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Endoscopy and low weights
text: Endoscopy and low weights Proposition LG5. The Galois representation of a specified endoscopic system [2, exposé 355]; [1, Thm. 2.2.3, §2.4] Let n ≥ 2 . Let f and g be normalized holomorphic cuspidal eigenforms of weights n + 2 and n , with the same finite-order nebentypus χ . At primes outside their levels write P_(f,p)(T) = 1 − aₚ(f)T + χ(p)p^(n + 1)T², P_(g,p)(T) = 1 − aₚ(g)T + χ(p)p^(n − 1)T². For a compatible coefficient embedding, let r_(f,λ) and r_(g,λ) be their two-dimensional Galois representations, normalized to have these arithmetic Frobenius polynomials. Then r_(λ) = r_(f,λ) ⊕︎ (r_(g,λ) ⊗ ε_(ℓ)) is symplectic with similitude character χ_(λ)ε_(ℓ)^(n + 1) , Hodge–Tate weights {0,1,n,n + 1} , and good-prime polynomial det (1 − r_(λ)(Frobₚ)T) = P_(f,p)(T)P_(g,p)(pT). Every continuous semisimple four-dimensional Galois representation with the same polynomials at all but finitely many primes is isomorphic to r_(λ) . Discussion LG5 describes the rank-four representation when the motivic spin parameter is the indicated endoscopic sum. It is a conditional identification of that eigenvalue system, not a nonvanishing theorem for every proposed pair of elliptic forms or every quaternionic level. The possible elliptic weights n + 2 and n also follow from the two real Weil-parameter exponents n + 1 and n − 1 in the proof of LG2. Cuspidal representations of a classical group can therefore have reducible spin Galois representations. At n = 2 , LG2 still gives Siegel weight (3,3) and hence Galois weights {0,1,2,3} whenever a cohomological cuspidal split transfer is available. The split-group Galois theorem includes this weight. What fails in the proof of LG3 is the automatic inner-form transfer criterion: the coefficient is trivial, and additional cohomological representations at infinity make the regularity hypothesis of Rösner–Weissauer Theorem 11.5 unavailable. Theorem 11.4 instead concerns an inner form compact modulo centre at infinity, so it cannot be substituted for our noncompact Sp(1,1) group. This leaves an additional transfer question for arbitrary general-type weight-two systems in this account; it is not a claim that Galois representations for them are impossible or unknown by every other method. The n = 1 Hardy limit has no coefficient E_(n − 2) and is outside LG3. Results for holomorphic limits of discrete series on the split group do not by themselves identify or transfer that quaternionic endpoint. It requires a separate global analysis. Finally, an eigenvalue system determines the semisimple Galois representation through its good-prime characteristic polynomials, but need not distinguish individual automorphic forms within a packet. These results do not give a bijection between all quaternionic eigenfunctions and all four-dimensional Galois representations.

title: Langlands parameters and Galois representations
heading: Geometric realization
text: Geometric realization Automorphic cohomology and geometric realization compares the quaternionic period construction with modular curves and universal abelian varieties. It gives the obstruction to a first-cohomology realization and distinguishes a real family of polarized fibres from the algebraic geometry used after transfer.
